node_definition.done_when: Read design/canvas-layout-spec.md for type scale and spacing, but note the canvas topbar was drawn against a three-project fixture and cannot hold twelve, so this departs from it deliberately on the lead's instruction. FIVE PARTS, one node because the whole point is that one preference propagates — splitting this across files is what produced the r-3col defect earlier today, where a container's rules were retired in one scope and the container survived in another. ONE: the topbar becomes a single row — brand, project control, tabs, search, settings, snapshot receipt — with the tabs left-aligned after the project control. TWO: the Overview tab is removed. The brand button already calls navProject(null) titled All projects and renders the fleet page, and CockpitBody renders the same cross-project content, so they are two doors to one room; fold anything CockpitBody shows that the fleet view does not into the fleet view rather than dropping it, and leave the tabs as the four within-project views Plans, Sprints, Graph and Crew. THREE: the project control shows the current project with its live dot and opens a dropdown listing only VISIBLE projects, each with its plan count and live count, plus a Configure entry at the foot. FOUR: Configure opens the visibility panel that lives in the settings menu in docs/ui/_shared.jsx beside theme and density, which already own exactly this class of cross-cutting display preference — the dropdown entry is a shortcut that opens that same panel and must not be a second implementation of it. The panel lists every mounted project with a visible or hidden toggle. FIVE: visibility propagates. It is read today only by shell.jsx for the chip strip; crew.jsx and the fleet strip never see it. Every fleet-wide display must respect it: the Crew run list, the Overview fleet statistics, and any other cross-project aggregate. Distinguish mounted from shown where a count is displayed, since twelve mounted and three shown are different facts. CRITICAL AND SUBTLE: hidden means excluded from aggregates and from the selector shortcut list; it must never mean unreachable. Any mounted project stays reachable through Configure and through the command palette — a project being hidden is why nova could not be selected, and that bug is a display preference wrongly used as a routing filter. A test asserts the topbar renders one row containing the tabs with no Overview tab, that the dropdown lists visible projects only and offers Configure, that Configure and the settings menu render the same panel rather than two, that hiding a project removes it from the Crew list and the fleet statistics while leaving it selectable through the palette, and that a count displaying mounted and shown reports both. The existing suite passes unchanged.
node_definition.goal: Make project visibility one fleet-wide setting that every surface respects, and fit the topbar on one row

node_definition.done_when: Two sessions independently watched finished runs display as working: one saw six nodes whose worker processes had all exited and whose manifests were all terminal on disk sit as '6 working' for 38 minutes with zero events, and one saw a run whose classifier read completed_unpromoted with a complete manifest while its phase still read starting. The mechanism is in reckon/crew/recovery.py and has two parts that compound. First, in classify_pointer around lines 186 to 196, when the process appears alive AND the log file's mtime is newer than the manifest's, the manifest is discarded wholesale: manifest_present set false, manifest_data emptied, manifest_status set to empty string. That staleness heuristic is right for a manifest written mid-run and then superseded, but it is wrong for a TERMINAL status: complete, blocked and failed are facts a later log line cannot undo, and discarding them is what erases the strongest completion signal available. Second, in _watch_snapshot around lines 556 to 578, state resolves to dispatched when phase is starting and the stall check that follows is gated on state being exactly working, while FLEET_WORKING_STATES at line 610 counts dispatched among the working bucket. So a run that dies before its phase advances is counted as alive and is permanently ineligible for the stall check. Fix both, leading with the manifest because it turns a timing question into a fact-on-disk question: never discard a terminal manifest status through the staleness path, and evaluate the stall check over every non-terminal state rather than working alone. Tests in tests/test_crew_finished_display.py assert: a pointer whose manifest reports complete while its log is newer and its process appears alive still resolves to a terminal state rather than dispatched, and the same for blocked and failed; a run killed immediately after dispatch, before its phase ever advances past starting, is still detected from its manifest alone; a run with no manifest and no activity past the stall window resolves to stalled from the dispatched state, which it cannot today; and a genuinely mid-run pointer whose manifest is non-terminal and whose log is newer still has that manifest treated as superseded, so the staleness heuristic is narrowed rather than removed. Your gate is that new test file plus tests/test_crew_recovery.py, tests/test_crew_ticker.py and tests/test_crew_watch_stream.py. Do NOT run the full suite and do NOT run any browser-driven test. That is the resumed-worker case and it is well exercised: this ledger holds 49 runs with attempt_kind resume, and three runs in this session alone went blocked then working after a resume. The distinction the previous change missed is that complete and failed are VERDICTS a later log line cannot undo, while blocked is a SOLICITATION that resume answers, and the discard is how the system notices it was answered. Narrow the exclusion set to complete and failed only, so a blocked manifest is discardable again under the unchanged surrounding conditions of an alive process and a newer log, while complete and failed remain protected as 1b7e72e intended. Add to tests/test_crew_finished_display.py: a blocked manifest with an alive process and a newer log resolves to working rather than blocked, named for the resumed worker it represents; a blocked manifest with a DEAD process or an older log still resolves blocked, so the fix does not simply delete the signal; and the existing complete and failed protections still hold, which the parametrised test already covers and must keep passing. Your gate is tests/test_crew_finished_display.py plus tests/test_crew_recovery.py, tests/test_crew_ticker.py and tests/test_crew_watch_stream.py, which were 28 passed at 8692c0aa245b82ed05ce46c108f6729abf261203. node_definition.done_when: reckon/crew/promotion.py appends the ledger row and deletes the live pointer, in that order so an interruption stays recoverable, and releases nothing else: the run's worktree survives until someone runs crew gc by hand and the worker process survives until it exits on its own. Measured on this workstation: 274 worktrees on disk against 458 promoted runs in one ledger, and a run observed process_alive true while its classification already read completed_unpromoted. Extend complete so that AFTER the ledger append and the pointer delete it also releases the run's own worktree and, if still alive, the run's own process group. Reuse the classification crew gc already applies in reckon/crew/routing.py rather than writing a second policy: a worktree is released only when git status --porcelain in it reports zero entries AND its HEAD is an ancestor of the integration branch as git merge-base --is-ancestor decides; a worktree failing either condition is left in place and never removed with force; and a shadow releases through the existing lineage rule against its committed record and retained patch. The process group is signalled only when a terminal manifest was delivered, because a live process with no manifest is a recovery case rather than a cleanup one. Every withheld release is named in the returned completion result with the condition it failed, so a retained worktree is visible at the moment it is created rather than discovered by a later path collision. A failure inside the release step must never undo or obscure the ledger append. Tests in tests/test_promotion_release.py assert: a promoted run whose worktree reports zero porcelain entries and whose HEAD is an ancestor of the integration branch leaves no worktree on disk and no live process, asserted through complete end to end rather than by unit-testing a helper; a promoted run whose worktree reports a porcelain entry keeps that worktree and names it in the result with the failed condition; one whose HEAD is not an ancestor of the integration branch does the same; a run with no terminal manifest is never signalled; and a simulated failure raised inside the release step still leaves the promoted ledger row intact and the run recoverable. The mechanism is in reckon/crew/recovery.py and has two parts that compound. First, in classify_pointer around lines 186 to 196, when the process appears alive AND the log file's mtime is newer than the manifest's, the manifest is discarded wholesale: manifest_present set false, manifest_data emptied, manifest_status set to empty string. That staleness heuristic is right for a manifest written mid-run and then superseded, but it is wrong for a TERMINAL status: complete, blocked and failed are facts a later log line cannot undo, and discarding them is what erases the strongest completion signal available. Second, in _watch_snapshot around lines 556 to 578, state resolves to dispatched when phase is starting and the stall check that follows is gated on state being exactly working, while FLEET_WORKING_STATES at line 610 counts dispatched among the working bucket. So a run that dies before its phase advances is counted as alive and is permanently ineligible for the stall check. Fix both, leading with the manifest because it turns a timing question into a fact-on-disk question: never discard a terminal manifest status through the staleness path, and evaluate the stall check over every non-terminal state rather than working alone. node_definition.done_when: The recovery order has been recorded in this workstation's guidance since the first incident and was not applied at the second, four hours later, by a different session - so guidance that must be recalled at the moment of an incident has already failed twice. It is now written where a coordinator is already reading. TWO FILES, AND THE LEAD DIRECTED BOTH. reckon/crew/AGENTS.md is the narrowest scope owning crew dispatch and the command surface, and gains a recovery section. A new reference under the ship skill's references directory carries the operational detail, linked from the skill's own text in the same beat so it is reachable rather than orphaned - read that SKILL.md before writing, and follow how its existing references are introduced. WHAT BOTH MUST STATE, and each claim below is measured rather than asserted, so reproduce the figures. THE CAUSE: a per-request provider refusal kills the turn without killing the session; the run classifies blocked, its worktree survives, and its session remains on disk. THE TRAP: session_id null on a live pointer means only that observe has not run, never that a run is unresumable - resume_plan recovers it from the stream by itself. Two coordinators read that null as a verdict on the same day; the first promoted five runs, the second left one blocked for five hours and forty-two minutes. THE ORDER: inspect the worktree for committed and uncommitted work, resume the session, and reconcile only once resume is impossible - because promotion deletes the pointer and takes the resume path with it. THE COUNTER-INSTINCTS, both of which are wrong and both of which were followed: promoting first to tidy the fleet destroys what you were about to recover; and re-observing a refused run to investigate a hold used to renew it, which is fixed but explains the habit. WHAT IS SAFE DURING A HOLD: observe reads the local stream and never calls the provider, so it works mid-refusal - confirmed on two sessions' runs tonight, and the opposite belief would teach a reader to panic when panic is unwarranted. THE AUTOMATIC PATH: a sweep resumes lapsed holds on a cadence from the follow loop, and a follower started before that code landed will never run it, so a follower is cycled when recovery code lands. THE COMMANDS as they exist when this lands, verified by running each with --help rather than copied from this brief, since two of them are being added by concurrent nodes and one existing crew recover does something else entirely. Do not restate the plan; link it. node_definition.done_when: THE TIMER IS SELF-EXTENDING AND A RETRY LOOP CANNOT CONVERGE. Measured tonight from this repository's committed ledger, data.holds: a claude dispatch hold opened 20:02:18Z and closed 23:52:19Z, held_seconds 13801, three hours fifty minutes on a lane that was serving. The control sits beside it - a claude-opus resume hold, held_seconds 83, closed the moment one served run reached that backend. The two differ only in whether traffic reached that specific backend. Every refused resume re-stamps the backend's budget record, so a caller retrying on any cadence shorter than the shelf life pushes the expiry ahead of itself, and observing the refused run does the same because its stream carries the rejection - the obvious check-before-believing move makes it worse. AVAILABILITY IS POLLED RATHER THAN READ FROM WRITTEN EVIDENCE, which is this workstation's standing direction, and this is the case that forces it: a timer answers only whether enough time has passed that a lane might serve, while one cheap request answers whether it does. Done when a hold whose refusal names no reset time is unknown-until-probed rather than exhausted-until-a-clock: the fence probes that backend with a minimal request and the probe's result, not the record's age, decides whether the wave opens. A served probe clears the hold and records the served observation so the next caller reads a fact rather than repeating the probe; a refused probe re-arms the hold and records that refusal as the new evidence. THE PROBE MUST NOT BECOME THE COST IT PREVENTS: rate-limited per backend so a wave of held dispatches issues one probe rather than one each, its result cached for a bounded interval that is itself configuration, and a backend that has never reported anything is still never held, because absence of a signal remains not evidence of exhaustion. node_definition.done_when: A crew follow process holds the module code it imported for its entire life. When a recovery sweep landed and was wired into that loop, every follower on this workstation had started hours earlier, so not one called it - two independent sessions were simultaneously unable to perform a recovery they had just gained, and one left a run blocked five hours forty-two minutes with its limit long lifted. The failure is silent in the costly direction: a stale renderer draws a wrong column and someone notices, while a stale follower recovers nothing and is indistinguishable from a fleet with nothing to recover. THREE SHAPES IN THE ORDER TO TRY THEM, and the plan states this order deliberately. First, the follower detects that the installed package on disk is newer than the one it imported and re-execs itself in place, preserving its session registration and its stdout so a watching pane sees no gap. Second, if in-place re-exec cannot preserve those, the watch seat publishes a version stamp each cycle and a follower reading a stamp newer than its own re-execs. Third, only if neither is achievable, the follower emits one line saying it is stale and how to cycle it - this is a fallback, not the answer, because the done-when requires an operator who never restarts a follower to still get new behaviour. Report which shape you implemented and why the earlier ones were not achievable if you fell back. THE DETECTION MUST NOT BE THE PACKAGE VERSION STRING: reckon's __version__ is dynamic via vcs and frozen at install, so it does not move when a working-tree edit lands - a watch-seat stamp built on it was already landed and measured inert across eighty-five commits. So the price is either a NEW NODE ID, which makes one piece of work appear as two unrelated ledger rows, or a MANUAL WORKTREE REMOVAL. BOTH PRICES ARE PAID IN THE CURRENCY THIS SYSTEM SPENT THE NIGHT PROTECTING: manual worktree removal is the act that turned a ten-minute provider outage into a loss of five recoverable sessions, and crew complete now refuses to promote a blocked run whose session is recoverable precisely to prevent it - so the switching path routes a careful operator toward the one action the rest of the system guards against. And crew resume accepts no backend override, so a run whose lane is genuinely spent cannot be continued elsewhere at all. That case is live: a run on another project is held by a usage limit resetting four days out, so resume never becomes available for it and a lane change is the only lawful move. THE SHAPE IS LOCKED as the plan's lane-change-verb decision: BOTH entry points over ONE implementation - a backend override on resume for a blocked run whose lane is spent, and a redispatch keeping the node id for a working run the coordinator wants elsewhere - because each covers a state the other cannot and two implementations would be two code paths able to disagree about one run. Done when a dispatched run moves to another backend keeping its node id, its worktree and its ledger identity, with no manual tree removal and no new node id; when the move records BOTH lanes and the reason on the run, so its history shows where it ran rather than appearing to have always run on the second; when a move onto a held lane is refused with the hold named, since the sweep's own rule is never to spend the last of a recovering quota; and when a session that cannot follow the move because the new backend is a different harness is reported as starting fresh rather than silently losing its context - that report is the load-bearing negative, because a silent context loss here is the same defect as a promotion reporting success while discarding a session. ASSERT THROUGH THE COMMANDS a coordinator invokes, over a dispatched run built the way dispatch writes one under a temporary config home with the real config home asserted untouched: the node id and worktree path unchanged afterwards, the ledger carrying both lanes, a move onto a held lane refused naming the hold, and a cross-harness move reporting the fresh start. Assert both entry points reach the same implementation. At least one added assertion must fail against base ff0a594. Measured over tests/test_crew_lane_change.py plus tests/test_crew_dispatch_guard.py in ONE invocation: zero failures against their combined count at base. Report ruff findings on the staged paths against the count at base.

Bisected: it passes at b06b68b^ and fails at b06b68b, the manifest-is-not-a-verdict change - so a run whose manifest reads complete and whose process has exited now classifies as ABANDONED rather than completed-unpromoted. THAT IS THE MOST EXPENSIVE MISCLASSIFICATION THIS SURFACE CAN PRODUCE and it is the inverse of the defect b06b68b was written to fix. Abandoned invites a coordinator to discard; completed-unpromoted invites them to promote; and such a run has finished work in its worktree that nobody has landed - so the label routes a reader toward destroying delivered work, which three separate guards were built this week to prevent. The live fleet is currently unaffected, measured at completed_unpromoted 1 and abandoned 0 across eleven real pointers, so the fixture reaches a manifest-and-liveness combination production does not - a latent regression rather than an active one, and not a reason to relax the fix. THE FIX MUST NOT UNDO b06b68b: a placeholder failed or blocked manifest must still render as running while the pid is alive, which is what that change bought and what a peer confirmed from two independent cases. Done when a run whose manifest status is complete and whose process has exited classifies as completed-unpromoted; when a placeholder failed manifest over a LIVE process still classifies as running, asserted so the earlier fix cannot be reverted by this one; when a run with no manifest and a dead process still classifies as abandoned, so that label stays reachable; and when the three-class fixture counts one of each. State in the code why complete over a dead process is a verdict while failed over a live process is not, because the asymmetry is the point and a later reader will otherwise flatten it. Record in reckon/crew/AGENTS.md that a node touching reckon/crew/recovery.py or reckon/mcp.py carries tests/test_ledger.py in its gate, since that module holds cross-cutting contracts - this classification count and the five-tool surface assertion - and has now caught two changes fenced away from it. node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_local_lane_refusal_signal.py -q passes, and a stream that died of rate limiting no longer reports that it carries no rate-limit event. THE DEFECT, measured tonight across four dead runs in two projects: reckon/_backends.py line 852 reads exactly one record kind for budget, "elif kind == rate_limit_event", and nothing in that module reads api_retry or error_status. The clive local backend never emits rate_limit_event. It emits api_retry records carrying error_status 429 and error rate_limit. So a run that died of rate limiting is recorded with budget detail "no rate-limit event in the stream yet", refusal false, headroom unknown. The documented rule is that unknown headroom never holds a wave, and correctly so, which means the fence cannot fire at any level of local exhaustion and the next wave dispatches into the lane that just shed workers. This is a guard that cannot fire, which outranks a guard that fires wrongly: a stale hold announces itself while a blind one is indistinguishable from a clear lane. THE SHAPES, measured rather than assumed. Exhaustion: many api_retry records then a terminal result record carrying subtype success together with is_error true. Mid-flight death: api_retry records and no terminal result record at all. DO NOT key on a retry count of ten. Ten is the retry budget for a single API call, not for a run; two dead runs here carry 15 and 18 api_retry records and two in another project carry 10 and 5, so any constant matches some exhaustions and misses others, which is the worst behaviour available to a fence. Read the count as a magnitude and the terminal shape as the verdict. THE FALSIFIER, and it is the assertion that matters most: retrying is not refusing. Two runs that completed normally tonight each carried SEVEN api_retry records and finished with real work committed. A change that treats any api_retry as a refusal would mark every busy lane spent and hold the whole fleet, and it would pass any test that only checks the dead runs. Assert both directions: a stream with retries that ends in a genuine success reports no refusal and does not hold; a stream whose retries end in the exhaustion shape reports a refusal with a stated reason naming rate limiting; a stream with no retries at all is unchanged; and the existing rate_limit_event path for other backends keeps working exactly as it does now. Measure base and head over tests/test_local_lane_refusal_signal.py plus every test importing reckon._backends; report failure ids either side and require none added.
node_definition.goal: Teach the budget observer to see the exhaustion signal the local lane actually writes, so a spent local lane can be known before the next wave enters it

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_closure_fence_agreement.py -q passes, and no pointer is reconciled on one surface and unreconciled on the other. THE DEFECT, measured by an imas-codex fleet and confirmed here at the source: two independent definitions of one word, neither consulting the other. reckon/crew/runs.py drain, around line 823, treats a pointer as reconciled when its recorded closure_disposition is handed-off, or still-working while its classification is running; for handed-off it consults neither age nor classification, and its docstring states that intent plainly, that a handoff remains valid until the receiving session reconciles the pointer. reckon/crew/recovery.py overdue_unreconciled_runs, around line 873, treats a pointer as unreconciled when its classification is completed_unpromoted or blocked and its terminal age exceeds the configured grace, and it never reads closure_disposition at all. So a terminal pointer past grace carrying a valid handed-off disposition is reconciled by drain and refused by dispatch with exit 6. That fleet measured exactly this on three pointers at once. WHY IT IS NOT A DISPLAY NIT: the ship skill instructs a coordinator to read the drain view and require unreconciled-runs zero before ending a session, so the fence a closure signature rests on is the permissive one. Their outgoing coordinator signed a sprint closure on that zero and committed it, attesting to a state the other surface denies. A fence satisfiable on one surface and refused on the other is not a fence. THE FIX: have overdue_unreconciled_runs consult the same recorded disposition drain does, through one shared predicate both call, so the two agree by construction rather than by two authors agreeing. Do not simply widen dispatch to ignore the pointers. THE PROTECTION THAT MUST SURVIVE, and these are the load-bearing assertions: a terminal pointer past grace carrying NO disposition is still refused by dispatch, because that is the forgotten-work case the fence exists for; a still-working disposition on a pointer that has since gone terminal excuses nothing on either surface, since drain already expires that and dispatch must not become the weaker of the two; and a handed-off pointer is reconciled on BOTH surfaces. Assert additionally that for a set of pointers mixing all three cases, the count drain reports and the count dispatch refuses on are equal. A change that merely relaxes dispatch would pass the third assertion and destroy the first. Measure base and head over tests/test_closure_fence_agreement.py plus every test importing reckon.crew.recovery or reckon.crew.runs; report failure ids either side and require none added.
node_definition.goal: Make the closure fence and the dispatch fence read one definition of unreconciled, so a session cannot be closed on a state dispatch denies

The mechanism is not ours to fix downstream: the harness retry budget is fixed at max_retries 10 with 5 to 39 second backoff, reckon passes no retry configuration and cannot extend it, so once a lane refuses long enough the turn errors and a print-mode process exits. node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_review_scoring.py -q passes, and the four artefacts below exist and are exercised by that file. WHY THIS EXISTS. A promoted run today carries a gate the worker wrote itself, which is why gate pass sits at 1.00 on every lane in the committed ledger and cannot separate one lane from another. An independent reader of the landed diff, run before the promotion decision rather than after it, supplies a second opinion the worker did not author. The local lane has the throughput to run one per landing. WHAT TO BUILD, all of it new files, none of it wired into dispatch or promotion in this node. FIRST, a persisted prompt file at reckon/crew/prompts/review.md holding the text a review worker is given. It is a file rather than a string inside a module so that it is versioned, diffable, and editable without a code change. It instructs the reviewer to read the source node goal, its done_when, its declared write paths, its manifest, and the diff of its commits against its base, and to emit one score from 0 to 20 for each of five named dimensions together with one sentence of justification per dimension citing a path or a line, plus a list of findings each naming a file and a line. The five dimensions are goal_fidelity, meaning the landed change does what the node goal states; evidence, meaning the gate measures what the done_when asserts and its result is recorded; scope_discipline, meaning the diff stays inside the declared write paths and carries nothing the goal does not imply; durability, meaning a test exists that fails if this change regresses; and fit, meaning the change matches the idiom of the code around it and introduces no name the repository naming rules forbid. SECOND, a schema in reckon/crew/review.py naming those five dimensions once, with the maximum of 20 stated once, so that a dimension added later is added in one place. THIRD, a parser in the same module turning a review worker emitted text into that schema. It accepts the emitted form the prompt asks for. It returns a value for every dimension the schema names. It does not average, weight, rank, or compare lanes; the total it reports is the arithmetic sum of what it parsed and nothing else. FOURTH, a durable store in the same module writing one review record per reviewed run under the reckon crew configuration directory, outside any run directory and outside any worktree, keyed by project and by the reviewed run id, with a read function returning it. The location must survive deletion of the run directory and of the worktree, because a measure that reads a file the cleaner removes decays to nothing. Every record carries the reviewed run id, the review run id, the reviewing backend and model, the timestamp, the parsed scores, the justifications, the findings, and the verbatim emitted text it parsed, so a later reader can re-derive the parse and see what was actually said. DO NOT WIRE IT. This node writes no call site in dispatch, promotion, recovery, or the ticker; those files are held by other workers in flight. It exposes the functions those call sites will use and nothing more. FALSIFIERS, each asserted in the test file. Emitted text missing one dimension parses to a record naming that dimension as absent, not to a total computed over four, because a total silently taken over fewer dimensions is a lower score indistinguishable from a worse one. A score outside 0 to 20 is refused with a message naming the dimension and the value rather than being clamped into range. The same three utilisations at 30 percent elapsed give known, and 96 and 99.5 are held. So a lane with almost none of its quota left is admitted for dispatch whenever the reading is taken early in its window, which is exactly when a burst of dispatches can spend the remainder. Before a7489798 those two rows were held. WHY THE EXISTING SUITE DID NOT CATCH IT. The falsifier written into that node required that each of the nine backends this project configures keep its held or clear verdict. The floors decide whether a projected exhaustion instant is emitted; they must not decide whether utilisation is a known reading. A reading carrying a utilisation figure has known headroom whether or not its burn multiple is admissible, and the ceiling comparison applies to it as it did before. Keep the emitted reason naming both facts, since a reader needs to know the utilisation was used and the projection was withheld. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. A reading at or above the ceiling is held at every elapsed fraction tested. A reading below the ceiling is not held at any of them. THE MEASUREMENT. reckon/crew/resumption.py declares DEFAULT_SWEEP_SECONDS 120.0, described in its own comment as short enough that a lane returning minutes later is picked up while the wave still matters. The status file at the recovery directory records swept_at 2026-09-06T15:08:27Z and swept_by_pid 4176213. That pid is a live crew follow process for this project, the producer is live, and four worker transitions were emitted to its pane at 15:18Z, 15:23Z, 15:38Z and 16:11Z. At 16:17Z the recorded sweep was 69 minutes old against a 120 second cadence. A second project reports the same shape: a run whose declared wait had been satisfied sat eligible for roughly 35 minutes with a live follower and no wake, and resume-ready run by hand picked it up at once. THE MECHANISM, in the follow loop in reckon/cli.py. The cadence gate is called at the top of the outer loop, once per outer iteration. The loop then opens the producer stream and enters an inner while True that reads lines, ticks, and sleeps. That inner loop never calls the cadence gate. It exits only when the follower is stopped or the producer stops being live. So while a producer stays up, the outer loop never iterates again and the sweep runs exactly once, at attach. The 120 second cadence is therefore not a cadence at all; it is a lower bound that only takes effect after a producer dies and the follower reattaches. A busy fleet and a quiet fleet are equally affected, because the inner loop is entered either way. WHAT TO CHANGE. The sweep must run on elapsed time while the follower is inside the stream read loop. Call the cadence gate from the inner loop on the same passes that already tick and sleep, so a follower reading a live stream sweeps on its declared interval. Keep the gate itself unchanged: it is already time since last sweep rather than a count of iterations, and it already guards against a tight poll becoming a hot path. Do not raise or lower DEFAULT_SWEEP_SECONDS, do not change what sweep does, and do not change the pane output; a sweep writes to the status file and the recovery log, and nothing about the follower belongs on the transition stream. WHY THIS IS NOT MERELY A MISSED WAKE. The sweep is what turns a parked run back into a running one, so a follower that stops sweeping converts every declared external wait into a manual operation while continuing to display as a healthy attached follower. The status file exists precisely because a sweep that ran and found nothing and a sweep that never ran are otherwise indistinguishable; that file is what made this measurable, and its stamp is the evidence above. A follower attached to a live producer stream that emits no lines for several cadence intervals calls the sweep once per interval, not once in total. A follower reading a stream that emits lines continuously calls the sweep on the cadence, so line traffic neither starves the sweep nor multiplies it. Two calls inside one interval produce one sweep, so the existing rate guard still holds from the inner loop. A sweep that raises does not end the follower and does not stop later sweeps. A stopped follower performs no sweep after it is stopped. The pane output for a given sequence of stream lines is byte-identical to the output before this change, asserted by comparing emitted lines with the sweep injected as a no-op. A second live run's pointer read the same. The classifier obtains liveness with record.get("process_alive"), a stored field. Every liveness-conditioned branch therefore evaluates against None rather than against the process. WHY THAT MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS. A deferral arm ahead of the manifest-status arms exists precisely so a terminal manifest word from a live worker is treated as a report in progress rather than an outcome; it is gated on alive is True. With the stored field reading None, that condition is false and the deferral does not apply, so the arm that exists to prevent a premature verdict is bypassed in exactly the case it was written for. A peer session measured the consequence: a worker wrote a placeholder manifest 40 seconds after dispatch, the follower emitted a terminal transition while the process was demonstrably alive on the same host, and the coordinator held that verdict for eighteen minutes. The arm was present, correct, and not reached. WHAT TO CHANGE. Establish liveness at the point of use. Where the reading host is the host that launched the run, ask the process table; the module that owns that question already exposes a function for it and already distinguishes a running process, a process owned by another user, a defunct entry, and an absent one. Where the launching host cannot be shown to be the reading host, do not ask, because a pid is meaningful only on the machine that issued it and this project's crew home is shared across login nodes, so asking there fabricates an answer in both directions. In that case use what is stored and carry forward that the answer is not proven. The stored field remains written as it is written today; this node changes which value the classifier consults, not what any writer records. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. Do not alter any classification arm, any classification name, the counter placement, or the action marker. Do not alter what the deferral does once its condition holds. Do not add a process lookup for any run other than the one being classified. Do not change how liveness is recorded onto a pointer. Do not treat an unprovable answer as death: that distinction is load-bearing here and elsewhere in this module. FALSIFIERS, asserted in tests/test_liveness_is_read_when_it_is_used.py. A pointer whose stored field says nothing, whose recorded launching host is the reading host, and whose pid names a running process classifies as though alive, and a terminal manifest word on that pointer does not become the classification. The same pointer with a pid naming no process classifies as though not alive. The same pointer with a pid naming a defunct entry classifies as though not alive, so this composes with the zombie narrowing landed in 8d856e9 rather than reintroducing the old answer. A pointer whose recorded launching host differs from the reading host is classified from its stored field alone, no process lookup is performed for it, and the result carries that the answer is unproven; assert the absence of the lookup rather than only its result. A pointer with no pid at all behaves as it does today. The classification for every combination of stored field and real process state is stated in the test as a table, so a later reader can see which of the two the code consults. Measure base and head over the new file and every test importing reckon.crew.recovery; report failure ids either side and require none added, noting the thirteen environmental failures in that set are equal on both sides.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_a_pointer_names_its_launching_host.py -q passes, and every live pointer written for a newly launched run records the hostname of the machine that launched it. WHY THIS IS OWED. A change landed at ab47256 makes the classifier establish liveness at the point of use rather than from a stored field, and gates that lookup on the pointer's launcher_host matching the reading host. Measured immediately after it landed: zero of nine live pointers carried that key, and no module in the repository writes it. So the gate is always false, the classifier keeps using the stored answer, and the landed change is inert. WHY THE GATE IS RIGHT EVEN THOUGH IT IS CURRENTLY EMPTY. The crew configuration home is on shared storage and the live-pointer directory is global across projects and machines. A pointer carries pid and pid_start_time and names no machine. So a reader on one login node computing liveness for a run launched on another asks its own process table about a pid that means nothing locally, and gets a fabricated answer in both directions: an absent pid reads as dead, which is the proof-of-death that a run needs before it may be called abandoned, and a reused pid reads as alive. The host gate is what makes the point-of-use read safe to perform at all; without the field the read cannot be enabled. WHAT TO CHANGE. When a run's live pointer is first written, record the hostname of the machine writing it, under the key the classifier already reads. Use the same spelling the reader uses so the two cannot disagree: the reader takes socket.gethostname(), so the writer takes socket.gethostname(). Record it once at launch rather than refreshing it, because it is a property of where the process was created and does not change while the process lives. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. Do not alter the classifier or any classification arm; the reader already exists and this node only supplies what it reads. Do not alter pid or pid_start_time. Do not backfill the field onto pointers already on disk: a pointer written before this change has no recoverable launching host, and inventing one would assert a fact nobody measured. Do not make the absence of the field an error anywhere; a pointer without it must behave exactly as it does today, because pointers written before this change will outlive it and a reader that refuses them would strand live runs. FALSIFIERS, asserted in tests/test_a_pointer_names_its_launching_host.py against a temporary configuration home, with an assertion that the real configuration home gains no file. A pointer written for a newly launched run carries the launching host, and its value equals what socket.gethostname() returns in the writing process. A pointer written and then re-read carries the same value, so the field survives the write-and-read cycle the classifier depends on. A pointer that predates this change, constructed without the field, is read without error and classifies exactly as it does today, asserted by comparing the classification against the same pointer processed before the change. The classifier performs a process-table lookup for a pointer whose recorded host equals the reading host, and performs none for a pointer whose recorded host differs, asserted by observing whether the lookup happened rather than only its result. A run whose pointer is rewritten during its life keeps its original launching host rather than acquiring the rewriter's. Measure base and head over the new file and every test importing reckon.crew.dispatch or reckon.crew.runs. Report failure ids either side and require none added. Do not run a census over the full importing set in one command: bound it per file, or gate only the files that cover the changed paths, because that set contains a test which does not complete in this environment and two nodes today ended without a manifest after backgrounding a long census.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_manifest_log_paths_are_durable.py -q passes, and a promoted run whose manifest cites a test log under the shared temporary directory is reported rather than recorded silently. THE MEASUREMENT, from this session's own promotions. Three separate workers wrote their test logs under the shared temporary directory despite the dispatch contract naming the run directory: their manifests cite paths beginning with the temporary root, and the coordinator noticed only while reading the manifests by hand. Two of the three were this coordinator's own nodes. WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS. Those logs are the evidence a promotion cites. A promoted ledger row names a gate command, an exit status and a log path, and the log path is what a later reader opens to check the claim. The shared temporary directory on this workstation is a small allocation that is cleared without notice, so a promotion can carry a citation to a file that no longer exists, and nothing distinguishes that from a citation to a file that was never written. The run directory persists with the run; the temporary root does not. WHAT TO CHANGE. Add a check over a manifest's cited log paths that reports any path resolving under the shared temporary root, naming the manifest, the key and the offending path. It reports; it does not refuse, rewrite or relocate anything. A path under the run directory, under the repository, or under any other durable location is not reported. The temporary root is what the standard library reports as the platform temporary directory, read from the running system rather than written as a literal, and a path is under it when its resolved form is contained by that resolved root, so a symlinked or relative spelling is caught rather than only a literal prefix. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. Do not alter promotion, the gate requirement, the ledger row, or any classification. Do not refuse a promotion on this finding: a coordinator promoting a run whose logs are already written cannot make them durable, and refusing would strand the record rather than improve it. Do not touch the manifest file. Do not check any path other than those a manifest cites as logs. FALSIFIERS, asserted in tests/test_manifest_log_paths_are_durable.py against constructed manifests and a temporary directory the test itself creates. A manifest citing a log under the platform temporary root is reported, and the report names the manifest, the key and the path. A manifest citing a log under the run directory is not reported. A manifest citing a log under the repository is not reported. A manifest citing no logs is not reported and does not raise. A manifest whose cited path does not exist on disk is judged by where it points rather than by whether it exists, because a missing durable path and a missing temporary path are different findings. A path that reaches the temporary root through a symbolic link or a relative spelling is reported, asserted by constructing such a path rather than by asserting on a prefix string. A manifest citing several logs of which one is under the temporary root reports exactly that one. The check reports and returns; no test asserts a refusal, and the absence of a refusal path is asserted rather than assumed. Measure base and head over the new file and every test importing the module you place the check in; report failure ids either side and require none added. Bound the run per file rather than issuing one census over every importing file.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_tool_arguments_accept_a_serialised_list.py -q passes, and a tool argument declared as a list is accepted when the client delivers it as a JSON text that parses to a list. THE MEASUREMENT, reported by a peer project. Five edit_plan calls in one evening were rejected with a validation error stating that ops should be a valid list, with input_type str and the input value shown as the serialised ops text. Structurally identical calls minutes apart succeeded. The peer's pattern: every rejection was an append to the comments target, or a batch containing one, with a body over roughly seven hundred characters; a resolve op and a followup append of similar length succeeded in the same minutes; shortening the body and removing parentheses did not change the outcome; the same content succeeded once on retry after a literal section sign was replaced with an escape, and failed three other times with no section sign present. So the correlation is with payload shape rather than with any one character, and the peer's reading is that the client hands the argument through as JSON text for some payloads. The consequence is that plan state cannot be written through that channel for long bodies; the peer preserved the record by writing it into the cumulative evidence document instead, so nothing was lost, but the comment channel was unreliable for an evening. WHERE TO FIX IT. reckon/mcp.py wraps each strict tool's argument model in a subclass carrying a before-mode validator that rejects unknown parameter names. That validator sees the raw incoming mapping before any field is coerced, and is the point where a serialised list can be recognised. WHAT TO CHANGE. When an argument declared as a list arrives as text that parses as JSON to a list, use the parsed list. Apply it to every argument the model declares as a list rather than to one named argument, because the variance is in how a client serialises and not in which tool is being called. Leave every other case to the existing validation so a genuine type error still reports as one. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. Do not alter the rejection of unknown parameter names, which is what that validator exists for. Do not coerce an argument the model declares as text, even when its content parses as JSON: an authored HTML argument can legitimately contain bracketed text, and rewriting it would corrupt a document rather than reject a call. Do not accept text that parses to something other than a list for a list argument. Do not accept text that does not parse. Do not change any tool's declared schema, so a client reading the schema still sees a list. FALSIFIERS, asserted in tests/test_tool_arguments_accept_a_serialised_list.py. A list argument delivered as JSON text produces the same result as the same argument delivered as a list, asserted by comparing the two outcomes rather than by asserting the call merely succeeded. A list argument delivered as JSON text that parses to a mapping is rejected, and the message names the argument. A list argument delivered as text that does not parse is rejected, and the message names the argument. A list argument delivered as an integer is rejected as it is today. AN ARGUMENT DECLARED AS TEXT WHOSE VALUE PARSES AS A JSON LIST IS PASSED THROUGH UNCHANGED, asserted on an authored HTML argument containing a bracketed list, because coercing it would corrupt a document. An unknown parameter name is still rejected with the existing message listing the accepted names. A tool's published schema still declares the argument as a list. Measure base and head over the new file and every test importing reckon.mcp; report failure ids either side and require none added. Bound the run per file rather than issuing one census over every importing file.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_figure_index_covers_animations.py -q passes, and a GIF under a project's figures directory appears in the Figures index with its real pixel dimensions, and adding one invalidates the discovery cache. THE MEASUREMENT, reported by a peer project and confirmed here by reading and running the code. A consuming project holds 48 GIFs against 437 PNG and SVG files, and every GIF is absent from the index while remaining fetchable by URL, so it is reachable and invisible. FOUR CALL SITES, each verified rather than taken on report. First, figure_rows in reckon/figures.py builds its inventory from two globs, one for png and one for svg, so a GIF produces no row. Second, the same function chooses a dimension reader with a two-way expression that reads the png reader when the suffix is png and the svg reader otherwise. A GIF therefore takes the svg branch, which reads a binary file as text with replacement and fails its regex, returning nothing. Confirmed by running that reader against a constructed GIF: it returns None while the file's own header states 640 by 480. That is a wrong answer rather than a loud one, which is why nobody saw it. Third, _discovery_signature in reckon/serve.py globs the same two extensions, so a newly written GIF does not change the signature. This one matters on its own: fixing the index without fixing the signature would look correct until somebody added a figure to a running server, at which point the index would not refresh. Fourth, the figure_rows docstring states one row per PNG or SVG. WHAT TO CHANGE. Include GIFs wherever those two extensions are gathered, in both files. Make the dimension dispatch three-way rather than two-way, so each format reaches a reader written for it and no format falls through to another's. Read a GIF's dimensions from its own header with no new dependency: the first six bytes are the signature GIF87a or GIF89a, and bytes six through nine are the logical screen width and height as little-endian unsigned shorts, so the reader checks the signature and unpacks those four bytes, in the same shape as the existing png reader. Update the docstring with the rest. WHAT NEEDS NO CHANGE, verified so the node does not widen: figures are served through the standard library's type guesser, which already reports image/gif, and the gallery thumbnail is a plain image element, which animates a GIF natively, so no frame extraction and no imaging dependency are required. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. Do not alter how titles or captions are resolved; that path reads a sidecar and is already format-agnostic. Do not alter the row shape, the ordering key, or the project segmentation. Do not add a dependency. Do not change what is served or how. Do not make an unreadable or truncated GIF raise: a file whose signature is absent or whose header is short reports no dimensions, exactly as a malformed PNG does today, because a figures index that refuses to render because one file is corrupt is worse than one row without dimensions. FALSIFIERS, asserted in tests/test_figure_index_covers_animations.py against a temporary figures tree the test creates. A GIF produces an inventory row, and that row carries the width and height from its header, asserted on a file whose dimensions are not square so a transposed unpack is caught. Both signature forms, GIF87a and GIF89a, are read. A PNG's dimensions and an SVG's dimensions are unchanged from what they are today, asserted on the same fixtures in the same test run so a three-way dispatch cannot have altered either. A GIF whose signature bytes are wrong yields a row with no dimensions and does not raise. A GIF truncated inside its header yields a row with no dimensions and does not raise. The discovery signature changes when a GIF is added to the tree and is stable when nothing changes, asserted by taking the signature twice around the addition rather than by inspecting the glob. Row count for a tree of one PNG, one SVG and one GIF is three. Measure base and head over the new file plus every test importing reckon.figures or exercising the discovery signature; report failure ids either side and require none added. Bound the run per file rather than issuing one census over every importing file.
node_definition.goal: Index a GIF figure with its real dimensions and invalidate the discovery cache when one is added, so an animation is not reachable and invisible

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_crew_ticker_layout.py -q passes with no failure added across the ticker's importing set, and model and effort occupy separate scannable cells whose width is reclaimed from separator padding rather than taken from the reason column. WHAT THE LEAD ASKED FOR, and this supersedes an earlier refusal. A previous attempt split the joined model-and-effort cell and was held, because the lead had not asked for the split. The lead has now asked for it, with two qualifications in their own words: the gap between model and effort must remain tight, and the gaps in the right-hand counter may be closed. So the split lands, and it lands without widening the row. THE STARTING POINT. The held commit is reachable as tag held-model-effort-split and carries the split with its width reasoning: the widest shipped model alias is ten characters and the widest effort word is seven. Take its approach rather than its text; it predates the whole-word role column now on the branch, which already spent nine columns on spelling documentation in full. TWO QUALIFICATIONS, STATED AS MECHANISM. Tight gap: the model cell is sized to the widest shipped alias and the effort cell follows it after a single space, so effort begins at the same column on every row while no row carries padding wider than the alias it holds. Alignment and tightness are the same requirement here rather than competing ones, because the column is sized to the content and not to a round number. Counter: the counter today renders each count as two right-aligned digits and a single letter, joined by a space, a middle dot and a space. Closing those gaps means the separator loses its surrounding spaces. The counted block must keep a constant width as counts change so the right edge of the row does not move, which is why the two-digit alignment stays. WHERE THE WIDTH COMES FROM. Reclaimed separator columns fund the model and effort cells. State in a comment what the row consumes after the change and against which budget, so a later reader adding a column knows what is left. The module's declared default width and the terminal width measured on this workstation, 208 columns, are both stated in the existing comments. The reason column must not shrink to fund this. THREE TESTS DELIBERATELY ENCODE THE JOINED CELL and must be updated rather than worked around: two in tests/test_crew_ticker.py and one in tests/test_crew_recovery.py, whose own text calls the joined form one routing fact rendered as one cell. Update each to state the new contract in its own words, that model and effort are two facts a reader scans in two columns, and keep every other assertion in those tests unchanged. Do not delete a test to make a suite pass. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. Do not alter which states exist, their names, their counter placement, the action marker, or the whole-word role rendering. Do not remove colour. Do not change what a transition carries. Do not shrink or truncate the reason column. FALSIFIERS. Effort begins at the same column offset on two rows whose model aliases differ in length, asserted on rendered rows rather than on a constant. No row places more than a single space between the end of the widest model alias and the effort word. A record carrying a precomposed joined model and effort string renders the same two cells as an equivalent record carrying them separately. The counter block occupies the same width for counts of 0, 9, 10 and 99, asserted across all four. The counter separator carries no surrounding space, asserted on a rendered row. The longest role word, the longest model alias and the longest effort word together do not exceed the stated budget. Colour codes are still emitted. Every dispatch role still renders whole. Measure base and head over tests/test_crew_ticker_layout.py, tests/test_crew_ticker.py, tests/test_crew_recovery.py, tests/test_fleet_counter_coverage.py and tests/test_external_wait.py; report failure ids either side and require none added.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_follow_observes_other_sessions.py -q passes, and one follower delivers transitions for its own session plus any number of named other sessions, registering delivery for its own session alone. WHAT THE LEAD ASKED FOR, in their words: extend the monitor to enable an attach to multiple sessions, because it is useful when tracking old work in addition to our own, and they suggested an appended session. WHY THE OBVIOUS IMPLEMENTATION IS UNSAFE, and this is the constraint the node exists to honour. The follow command's session option does two things, not one: it narrows delivery to the runs that session dispatched, AND it registers the session as attached. Dispatch refuses a session whose runs would finish unheard, and that refusal is decided on the attachment record. So a follower that registered attachment for a second session would satisfy the OTHER coordinator's dispatch precondition with delivery that ends when this session ends. Their guard would read as cleared while the thing it guards against became true, which is the failure this fleet has spent a night removing: a guard satisfied by evidence that does not mean what it claims. WHAT TO CHANGE. Keep the existing session option exactly as it is: one value, the owning session, narrowing delivery and registering attachment. Add a separate repeatable option naming other sessions to observe. Transitions for an observed session are delivered to the pane. Nothing is registered for an observed session: no attachment record, no delivery claim, no effect on any dispatch guard anywhere. Say in the option's help text that observing does not vouch for delivery, so a reader of the command line knows which half they are getting. A row from an observed session is marked as another session's, and the ticker already carries a marker for exactly that meaning; use it rather than inventing a second spelling. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. Do not alter what the existing session option does, its name, or its registration. Do not alter the producer seat, its arming, or the watcher record. Do not alter which transitions are emitted for the owning session. Do not add a way to observe every session at once: the lead asked to name old work alongside their own, and an all-sessions mode would deliver another fleet's whole history into a pane sized for one coordinator's attention. Do not change the ticker's column widths or its marker's spelling; if the marker turns out to need a change, block and say so rather than reaching outside the fence. FALSIFIERS, asserted in tests/test_follow_observes_other_sessions.py against constructed pointers and a temporary configuration home, with an assertion that the real configuration home gains no file. A follower given an owning session and two observed sessions delivers transitions for all three. The attachment record names the owning session only, asserted by reading the record rather than by reading the command's output. A dispatch guard consulted for an observed session reports no delivery, asserted through whatever the guard reads rather than by asserting on the follower. A follower given no observed sessions behaves exactly as it does today, asserted against the same expected lines as the existing single-session case. Rows from an observed session carry the other-session marker and rows from the owning session do not. An observed session named identically to the owning session does not produce duplicate rows for one transition. An observed session that dispatched nothing yields no rows and no error. Naming an observed session does not change what any other session's dispatch is permitted to do, asserted by checking the guard for a third session that was neither owned nor observed. Measure base and head over the new file plus every test importing reckon.cli or reckon.crew.runs; report failure ids either side and require none added, and bound the run per file rather than issuing one census, because that set contains a test which does not complete in this environment.

node_definition.done_when: The document docs/research/deploy-matrix.html carries the topology measurements below, each with its observation date and its derivation, and no figure is presented in a form that invites the misreading its source warns about. WHAT ARRIVED, from the session that owns the deployment, measured today from each engine's own startup report. Per topology at a max model length of 1,048,576: the four-card topology reports a KV pool between 2,554,833 and 2,557,835 tokens with a kv_cache_max_concurrency of 2.44; the two-card topology reports 1,173,125 tokens with 1.12. Per-request decode is 23.3 tokens per second on four cards and 23.1 on two. Prefix cache is 17.0 percent cumulative over the four-card window. THE TWO CAVEATS ARE THE POINT, NOT FOOTNOTES. First, kv_cache_max_concurrency counts requests at the maximum context length, not sessions. At the roughly 83,000 tokens an agentic worker actually holds, four cards fit about thirty concurrent and two cards about fourteen. A matrix that recorded 2.44 as two concurrent workers would understate capacity by an order of magnitude, and that is the specific misreading the measuring session asked to have prevented. Record the raw figure, record what it counts, and record the derived figure at realistic context beside it with the 83,000 stated as the assumption it is. Second, the four-card pool differed by about 3,000 tokens between two launches of the SAME profile, so it is approximate and must not be written as a constant to assert against; state the range and the fact that it moved between launches. THE ROW THE MEASURING SESSION MOST WANTS CARRIED: per-request decode is unchanged between the two topologies, 23.3 against 23.1. Cards buy pool and long-context headroom, not speed. State it as the finding it is, because it is the row people assume the other way. A ZERO-DOWNTIME ROTATION IS NOW DEMONSTRATED RATHER THAN REASONED. Four cards to two to four across one day; the second rotation had no dark window because the new topology came up on its own port while the old kept serving, the router preferred it on card count, and only then did the old one stop. Record that traffic moves on health rather than on a timer, so an engine that never becomes reachable leaves the old one serving. Record that this rests on two properties first exercised with two real serves up today: the router collapsing a duplicate model identifier onto the widest topology, which previously returned a conflict on every request, and the endpoint document republishing on both serve and shutdown, which tracked a port moving 18800 to 18809 to 18800 across two rotations with no operator step. A DEFECT THAT DESERVES ITS OWN ROW BECAUSE IT IS NOT ABOUT CAPACITY. A consuming project had its client address pinned to a serve port and was unable to run for hours during the two-card window while the model served normally, because its gate treats an unreachable compose endpoint as fatal to the entire run, so unrelated pools refused to start. The cause was documentation naming a serve port under a heading about what to point a client at. The rule to record: only the router address is stable; a serve port belongs to a profile at a topology and rotates. WHAT TO CORRECT. If the document carries a prefix-cache figure near thirty percent, replace it with 17.0 percent cumulative and state the window, because the earlier figure was generalised from three early spot readings on a warm working set and the cumulative figure is roughly half. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. Do not alter any existing measured cell, its date or its derivation. Do not convert a cell marked unmeasured into a measured one unless this message supplies the measurement. Do not restate the ledger filters in section eight. Do not add a lane, remove a lane, or change the row-per-backend shape. Do not present any capacity figure as a ceiling: this document's own discipline is that a lane ceiling belongs to its deployment and is discovered rather than assumed, and these figures are capacity reports from a startup log, not probed limits. FALSIFIERS. Every figure added carries its observation date and how it was obtained. The raw concurrency figures appear only beside a statement of what they count. The derived thirty and fourteen appear only beside the 83,000-token assumption they rest on. The pool figure appears as a range with the between-launch variation stated. No sentence claims cards increase per-request speed. The rotation account names health rather than elapsed time as what moves traffic. The address rule names the router as the only stable address. Any prefix-cache figure in the document reads 17.0 percent with its window. The document still parses as the reckon research type it declares, with its existing meta unchanged.

node_definition.done_when: grep for the phrase durable write in skills/reckon-ship/references/worker-protocol.md and confirm the file states that a worker commits at each deliverable and writes its manifest before beginning any long output or any wait, with the measured reason beside it; then confirm the file still contains its existing manifest-path and delivery sections unchanged by diffing those sections against the previous revision. THE MEASUREMENT, compiled across two fleets on one locally served lane and reported independently by three sessions. Forty runs. On the reporting fleets, small-scope code-changing nodes with a named check landed and scored 9 or 10 out of 10 in independent review, while broad-reading and report-shaped nodes died late with a response that stopped arriving or a request that timed out. One fleet: implement 8 of 8 passed, conformance reviews 7 of 7, investigate scouts 0 of 5. The other: code-changing nodes 5 of 6, report-shaped nodes 3 of 8. THE MECHANISM, AND TWO EARLIER EXPLANATIONS WERE WITHDRAWN BEFORE THIS ONE. A tokens-per-second discriminator held on 14 runs and did not reproduce on 26, where passes ran 1.69 to 6.54 output tokens per second and failures 1.79 to 6.12, so the reporting session retracted it and recommends no rate-based abort rule. A context-accumulation explanation was also withdrawn and inverted by the larger sample: per-turn context was HIGHER in the survivors, 107,000 to 215,000 input tokens per turn against 41,000 to 101,000 in the dead scouts, and the largest run of all passed at 173 turns and 37.1 million cumulative input tokens. Turn count and cumulative input separate nothing. What survives both samples is narrower: the failure is a long single output late in a long session under load. Neither fleet lost a node whose brief made the deliverable a small, early, incremental write. Two partial survivors are the evidence: one wrote its findings into its manifest and then died before its report, so the findings survived; another committed and then died, so the commit survived. Both survived because the durable write came before the long output. Four total losses each had the report as one final generation. WHY THE LANE MAKES THIS WORSE RATHER THAN CAUSING IT. Every stream in both fleets carries a prompt-cache read of zero and a cache creation of zero, so context is re-sent in full every turn; the heaviest node re-sent 37.1 million input tokens across 173 turns. A broad brief on this lane is therefore not merely slower, it is self-terminating. WHAT TO ADD TO THE FILE. State that a worker commits at each deliverable rather than once at the end, and writes its manifest before beginning any long output and before any wait. State the reason as measured rather than as advice: a durable write that precedes the long generation survives the generation failing, and every total loss in forty runs had its deliverable as one final output. State that this is why a node whose deliverable is a report should write that report incrementally to its file as it is produced, rather than composing it in one closing generation. Keep the existing rule that long output goes in the file and the reply is the path, and connect the new text to it rather than restating it. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. Do not alter the eight node properties or their order. Do not alter the manifest-path section, the delivery section, or the fence descriptions. Do not add a rate-based abort rule, a turn-count limit, or a context-size limit: all three were measured and none discriminates, and the file must not acquire a threshold the data refutes. Do not name a backend, a model or a lane: the property is about where the durable write falls relative to the long output, and a file naming this lane would read as inapplicable on another. node_definition.done_when: The document docs/research/deploy-matrix.html states that the glm lane is withdrawn with its date and reason, carries the effort-versus-durable-cost figures below, and carries the spark profile below; then grep the file and confirm the glm rows are marked withdrawn rather than deleted, and confirm no sentence recommends a lower effort for any node class. THREE CHANGES, ALL MEASURED, ALL DATED 2026-09-08. FIRST, THE GLM LANE IS WITHDRAWN. The lead has dropped it: the model does not fit the serving deployment alongside capacity for other work. Mark the lane withdrawn with that reason and date. Do not delete its cells and do not scrub its rows from the matrix, because a withdrawn lane that was measured is a record and a reader comparing lanes later needs to know it existed and why it went. State alongside it that the lane was never cleanly measured: nine rows, zero passing, and the classifications were six malformed-node and three infrastructure-failure, so two thirds were coordinator brief defects and the remaining three trace to a window defect on that lane. The honest cell is not that the model performed poorly; it is that no clean measurement of it exists. SECOND, EFFORT DOES NOT WANT A DISPATCH KNOB, AND THE MEDIAN HIDES WHY. Measured on the committed ledger over the sol model, which carries the only two-effort sample large enough to compare: at high effort 266 runs, 246 durable, 92 percent, median wall 568 seconds, total wall 38.2 hours, and 558 seconds of wall per durable node. At medium effort 236 runs, 207 durable, 88 percent, median wall 492 seconds, total wall 48.6 hours, and 846 seconds of wall per durable node. So medium is faster per run by median and 52 percent dearer per durable node, and it consumed more total wall while producing fewer durable nodes. State the median beside the per-durable figure precisely because the median inverts the conclusion, and a reader who sees only the median will route to the wrong effort. The finding to record is that effort trades turns rather than buying quality, and the unit-of-work cost favours a uniform high effort over a routing knob. WHAT MUST NOT BE OVERSTATED IN THAT CELL. Generated tokens per durable node run the other way, 6.9 thousand at high against 3.6 thousand at medium, and generation is not what a subscription meter charges. Cumulative input per run is not recorded anywhere in the ledger, only a peak, so the exact quota cost per durable node is unmeasured and must be marked so. node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_quota_weight.py -q passes, and a function in a new module converts a run's model identity and its token quantities into a relative quota weight that discriminates the members of one metered model family, refusing rather than defaulting for a model it has no declared rate for. WHY. This fleet routes almost everything to one member of a metered family and is struggling with its weekly ceiling, while two cheaper members of the same family are measured as finishing comparable nodes. Nothing in the harness records how much quota a run actually consumed relative to another, so every routing argument is currently made on wall clock, which is not what a quota is spent in. The figures below were read from the vendor's published rate card and must be carried in the module as a declared table with the reason beside it, because a rate this table gets wrong silently misroutes every future node. THE DECLARED RATES, per million tokens, as published. The family's strongest member: input 4.00, output 20.00. Its middle member: input 2.00, output 12.00. Its efficient member: input 0.20, output 1.20. So relative to the strongest member, the middle member costs half on input and three fifths on output, and the efficient member costs one twentieth on input and six hundredths on output. There is a fourth, smaller member this project also dispatches to, on a separate quota, for which NO published rate was found; it must return the explicit refusal below rather than be assigned a plausible number. THE SURCHARGE, which is the part no surface here models. A request whose input exceeds 272,000 tokens is charged at twice input and one and a half times output FOR THE WHOLE REQUEST, not for the tokens above the line. So the weight depends on how many of a run's requests crossed that line, which is not derivable from a cumulative total: eighty requests of 200,000 tokens sum to sixteen million and cross nothing, two requests of 300,000 sum to 600,000 and cross twice. Take the threshold and both multipliers as named module-level constants with the published rule in a comment. WHAT TO BUILD, IN A NEW MODULE ONLY. Create reckon/crew/quota_weight.py exposing one function taking a model identifier, cumulative input tokens, cumulative output tokens, and the number of requests whose input crossed the threshold, and returning the relative weight together with the rate entry it used and whether the surcharge was applied. Do not import from reckon.crew.metering, which a peer is writing this hour; take plain numbers so this module is testable and reviewable on its own. Do not wire it into promotion, dispatch, the ledger, the CLI or any surface. Do not read any ledger file. THE UNIT MUST BE STATED AND MUST NOT BE DOLLARS. This project's workers run on a subscription, and the vendor states explicitly that a subscription is not priced per token; the published rates are the token-denominated billing surface and are being used here only as a RATIO between family members. So the function returns a dimensionless weight relative to the family's strongest member at one, never a currency amount, and the module docstring must say that in one sentence and say why. A corroborating figure worth recording in the same docstring: the subscription's own per-window message allowances for these three members stand in a ratio of roughly one to two to twenty, which agrees in direction and in order of magnitude with the token ratio, so the two independent denominations do not contradict each other. AN UNDECLARED MODEL IS A REFUSAL, NOT A DEFAULT. A model identifier absent from the declared table returns an explicit unknown carrying the identifier it could not price, and the caller can see that it was not priced. Never fall back to the strongest member's rate, never fall back to an average, and never return zero: this project has a standing rule that a free or unmeasured lane recorded as zero cost makes it look like the dearest or the cheapest lane on any surface that ranks by cost, and the existing ledger deliberately nulls and flags such a value rather than imputing it. Follow that precedent. FALSIFIERS, asserted in tests/test_quota_weight.py, every expected figure computed in the test from the declared constants rather than written as a literal. Equal token quantities across the three declared members return weights in the published ratio, with the strongest member's weight exactly one. THE ORDERING IS STRICT: for any identical non-zero token quantities the middle member's weight is strictly less than the strongest member's and the efficient member's is strictly less than the middle member's, so a future rate edit that accidentally inverts the family is caught. A run with zero requests over the threshold and a run with one differ by exactly the surcharge the constants declare, and the surcharged weight is strictly greater. A run whose cumulative input is sixteen million across many small requests, with zero crossings, weighs LESS than a run whose cumulative input is six hundred thousand across two crossing requests on the same model, asserted against figures the test computes, because this is the case a cumulative-only reading gets backwards and the whole reason the crossing count is a parameter. An undeclared model identifier returns the unknown marker, carries the identifier, and does not raise. An undeclared model does not return zero and does not return the same value as any declared member, asserted directly. Zero tokens on a declared model returns zero weight, since nothing was consumed, and this is distinguishable from the undeclared unknown. A negative token count raises rather than returning a negative weight. Measure base and head over the new file and the tests that import reckon.crew, report failure ids either side, require none added, bound the run per file, and never run the full suite for this node.
