node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_input_token_quantities.py -q passes, and the throughput block a run records carries the largest single request's input tokens and the run's cumulative input tokens in two separately named fields, with neither dialect ever filling one from the other. WHY. reckon/_backends.py has one field, peak_input_tokens, carrying two different quantities depending on which backend wrote the row, and the module states the rule it breaks in its own docstring. The method that serves the claude and clive dialects says, verbatim: Peak input is the largest single prompt the run sent, which is the figure a context window is actually spent against; the cumulative totals on the result are the sum over every request and would read far past any window. The method that serves the codex dialect then computes peak_input as a SUM over the run's usage counters, input tokens plus cached input tokens, and stores that sum in the field named peak. Measured across 3,269 ledger rows in the mounted projects: the codex figure has a median of 16,385,195 and a maximum of 106,803,531 while the clive figure's median is 171,518 and claude-opus's is 135,558. No context window is sixteen million tokens, so the codex column is not a peak and every surface that reads it as one is wrong. WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS. A published rule charges a request whose input exceeds 272,000 tokens at twice input and one and a half times output for the whole request, so the largest single request is what decides whether a run paid a surcharge, and the sum cannot answer it in either direction: eighty requests of 200,000 sum to sixteen million and never cross, two requests of 300,000 sum to 600,000 and cross twice. Both shapes occur here. Separately, input_utilisation_pct is computed from this field against the input budget, so on any dialect where the field holds a sum that percentage is a cumulative-over-window ratio and means nothing. WHAT TO CHANGE. Give the shared throughput block a cumulative input field and a cumulative cached input field alongside the existing peak field, defaulting to the unmeasured marker the block already uses for everything it did not measure, and thread them through the block constructor and the block that admits it measured nothing so both shapes carry the same keys. In the codex dialect, record the summed counters into the cumulative fields where they belong, and record the peak field as the unmeasured marker rather than as the sum, because that dialect's result does not report a per-request maximum and an honest absence is worth more than a wrong number. Do not attempt to derive the per-request maximum here: it needs a walk over per-turn records, another node owns that, and guessing it in this file is how the present defect was introduced. In the claude and clive dialect, keep the existing peak derivation exactly as it is and populate the cumulative fields from the result's own cumulative totals if and only if the result reports them; where it does not, leave them unmeasured. Compute input_utilisation_pct from the peak field only, so it becomes unmeasured on the codex dialect rather than misleading, and say why in a comment at the computation. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. Do not touch reckon/crew/promotion.py or reckon/crew/prompts.py, both held by peers. Do not rewrite existing ledger rows or add a migration: the historical codex column keeps its recorded value under whatever name the field ends up with, and a reader of old rows is served by the finding being documented, not by a rewrite this node cannot verify. Do not add the surcharge multiplier or any cost arithmetic; this node records quantities and another owns their price. FALSIFIERS, asserted in tests/test_input_token_quantities.py. A constructed codex-dialect stream carrying known input, cached input and output counters produces a throughput block whose cumulative input equals the sum the test computes from those counters, whose cumulative cached input equals the cached counter, and WHOSE PEAK INPUT FIELD IS THE UNMEASURED MARKER, so the sum can never again be read as a peak. A constructed claude-dialect stream with three assistant turns of differing input sizes produces a peak input equal to the largest of the three and not their sum, asserted against figures the test computes. The block returned by the constructor and the block that admits it measured nothing carry exactly the same set of keys, asserted by comparing the key sets, so no reader meets a block missing a field. input_utilisation_pct is the unmeasured marker whenever the peak field is unmeasured, even when a cumulative figure and an input budget are both present, so the ratio cannot be computed from the wrong numerator. A block where peak input is present and below the input budget still reports the same percentage it reports today, asserted against a figure the test computes, so the existing meaning is unchanged on the dialect that was correct. Every existing test that asserts on a throughput block still passes: run the tests that import the backends module and the tests that assert on ledger throughput rows, measure base and head over that set, report failure ids either side, and require none added. Bound the run per file rather than issuing one census, and never run the full suite for this node.

WHY THIS IS THE BLOCKING GAP. Every routing and cost decision this fleet is making rests on tokens per durable node, and the ledger records a PEAK input figure and no cumulative one. The reason to include them is that the meter on at least one metered lane charges total input including cached, which this project has recorded; the reason a reader might expect otherwise is that a cache hit feels free. Return an explicit unmeasured marker rather than zero for the first three. This project has repeatedly been misled by a zero standing in for an absence, and a cost figure that reads zero for an unmeasured run would understate a lane on every surface that sums it. A constructed stream in each dialect returns the exact sums of the counters it contains, asserted against figures computed in the test rather than against constants. node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_rollout_receipt.py -q passes, and a function in a new module reads, for one run identified by its session id, the quota and token receipt the metered client already writes to its own per-session rollout file: the run's true cumulative input across every turn, the largest single request it sent, how many of its requests exceeded 272,000 input tokens, the effective context window the client reported, and the run's position in its rolling quota window. WHY THIS IS THE MOST VALUABLE NODE AVAILABLE. This fleet is rationing a weekly quota and has been reasoning about it from wall clock and from a mislabelled token column, while the client has been writing the actual quota reading into a file on this machine on every single request. Nothing in this project reads that file. A peer established the route this hour and it is verified: the client keeps one rollout file per session under its own sessions directory, the file name contains the crew session id verbatim, and its records carry the figures below. This is not a modelled cost, it is the vendor's own accounting handed to us. THE RECORD SHAPE, verified on this host so you do not need to discover it, though you must confirm it rather than trust me. Records of interest have a payload whose type is token_count. That payload carries an info object holding total_token_usage and last_token_usage, each with input_tokens, cached_input_tokens, cache_write_input_tokens, output_tokens, reasoning_output_tokens and total_tokens; info also carries model_context_window. The payload additionally carries a rate_limits object with a primary object holding used_percent, window_minutes and resets_at, and a credits object. Measured: window_minutes is 10080, which is seven days, so primary is the weekly quota and used_percent is our position in it. total_token_usage is the run's running total across every turn, which is the figure a peer proved the existing ledger column understates on any resumed run, and last_token_usage is the most recent single request, which is the figure this dialect's crew stream cannot supply at all. WHAT TO BUILD, IN A NEW MODULE ONLY. Create reckon/crew/rollout.py exposing one function that takes a session id, locates that session's rollout file, and returns the cumulative input, cumulative cached input and cumulative output from the LAST total_token_usage record; the maximum input over every last_token_usage record; the count of last_token_usage records whose input exceeded the threshold; the effective context window; and the quota window's used_percent, window_minutes and reset time from the last record that carries them. Take the threshold as a named module constant with its published rule in a comment. Do not wire it into promotion, dispatch, the ledger, the CLI or any surface. Do not read or modify any configuration file. Do not edit reckon/_backends.py, reckon/crew/metering.py, reckon/crew/quota_weight.py, reckon/crew/context_budget.py, reckon/crew/promotion.py, reckon/crew/prompts.py or docs/research/deploy-matrix.html; peers hold all seven this hour. THE BOUNDARY WITH A PEER, so you do not duplicate it: another node derives cumulative tokens from the CREW STREAM and correctly reports the per-request maximum as unmeasurable there. Your module reads the CLIENT'S ROLLOUT instead, which does carry it. Both are correct and they are different surfaces; say so in your docstring and name the other surface, so a reader meeting one knows the other exists. THE QUANTISATION CAVEAT IS PART OF THE DELIVERABLE, NOT A FOOTNOTE. Measured across twenty-four runs today, used_percent is reported only as whole numbers, so a single run's consumption comes back as zero, one, two or three points and a run that truly cost four tenths of a point is indistinguishable from one that cost nothing. Per-run attribution from this field is therefore not sound and per-model aggregates over many runs are. State that in the docstring in those terms, and return the raw reading rather than a computed per-run delta, so no caller can accidentally attribute a single run's burn from a quantised figure. This project already carries the same reasoning elsewhere for a burn projection floor: below a few percent of a window, quantisation dominates the measurement. Do not invent a floor here; just refuse to compute the delta. AN ABSENT RECEIPT IS NOT A ZERO. A session id with no rollout file, a rollout file that cannot be read, a file carrying no token_count record, and a file whose records carry no rate limits are four different states and must not collapse into one another or into zero. Return an explicit unmeasured marker for each figure the file does not support, and never return zero for a figure that was not measured: a quota reading of zero means an untouched window and is a real and different fact from an unread file. FALSIFIERS, asserted in tests/test_rollout_receipt.py, every expected figure computed in the test rather than written as a literal, and every fixture constructed rather than borrowed from a real session except where stated. A constructed rollout whose last_token_usage records carry differing input sizes returns the LARGEST, not the first, not the last, and not their sum, asserted against a fixture whose total is much larger than its maximum so a sum cannot pass. A constructed rollout carrying three requests above the threshold and four below returns three. A constructed rollout with several total_token_usage records returns the LAST one's figures, not the first and not a sum of them, since the field is already cumulative and summing it would double count; assert against a fixture whose earlier totals are smaller. The returned maximum single request is strictly less than the returned cumulative input on any fixture with more than one request, which is an arithmetic invariant and catches a confusion between the two objects. A missing session id, an unreadable file and a file with no token_count record each return the unmeasured markers and do not raise. A constructed rollout reporting a used_percent of zero returns zero and NOT the unmeasured marker, asserted directly against the unmeasured case, because those two are the states this project most often conflates. RANGE ONE FALSIFIER OVER THE REAL POPULATION, deliberately: run the function over at least twelve real session ids taken from this project's own ledger rows, assert it raises on none, and assert that for every run where both figures are measured the maximum single request does not exceed the reported effective context window, which is a physical invariant and the strongest available check that you are reading the right field. Report how many of the twelve had a rollout file at all, because a low hit rate is itself a finding about retention. Measure base and head over the new file and the tests that import reckon.crew, report failure ids either side, require none added, bound the run per file, and never run the full suite for this node.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_lane_evidence.py -q passes, and a function in a new module returns, for a stated node shape, one row per lane carrying the three metrics that discriminate lanes plus the sample size behind each, refusing to report any figure whose sample is below a declared floor. WHY THESE THREE AND NOT THE OBVIOUS ONE. An orchestrator choosing a lane today has wall clock and folklore. The obvious metric, gate pass rate, CANNOT route and must be excluded with its reason stated in the module docstring: the worker writes its own gate, so the rate is saturated between 0.93 and 1.00 across every lane measured in this project and carries almost no information. Three metrics do discriminate and all three are derivable from the ledger rows this project already commits. FIRST, REWORK. A durable node is one whose run promoted with a commit. A node is reworked when a LATER run re-touches any path the earlier run declared as a write path. Measured previously in this project, rework discriminates about eight times more strongly than gate pass and reverses the cost ordering: one lane looks 34 percent cheaper on gate pass and is 22 percent dearer per durable node once rework is counted. Compute rework by comparing declared write paths across rows ordered by dispatch time, and exclude a row's own attempts and its own shadows from counting as rework of itself, since a retry of one node is not the next node redoing it. SECOND, OVERCLAIM, which is the metric today's evidence most needs and which nothing computes. A row overclaims when the worker's manifest reported a terminal success while the coordinator's recorded outcome says the done-when was not met. The rows carry both: the manifest status, and the promoted outcome and failure classification. Count a row as overclaiming when its manifest status was complete or passed and its promoted classification is work-rejected, or when its outcome text records that a named part of the done-when was absent, unexecuted or not delivered. Do not attempt to judge the work yourself and do not parse the done-when; read only what the coordinator recorded. This is the metric that separates a lane that stops and says so from a lane that stops and reports complete, and those two failure shapes need opposite handling from an orchestrator. THIRD, COST PER DURABLE NODE, expressed in the dimensionless lane weight this project already declares rather than in currency, since the workers run on a subscription that is not priced per token. Take the weight from the existing reckon.crew.quota_weight module; do not recompute any rate and do not import reckon.crew.rollout or reckon.crew.metering, whose figures are not yet on the rows. Where a row carries no token quantities, the cost for that row is unmeasured and it must not be counted as zero, because a lane with unmeasured rows would otherwise rank as the cheapest. Report wall seconds per durable node beside it as the fourth column, since wall and quota are different scarce things and an orchestrator trades them against each other. CONDITION EVERY ROW ON NODE SHAPE, because the premise of the whole surface is that the best lane depends on the work. Take the shape as the role and the specification level, and return only rows matching them, so a caller asking about exact implementation nodes is not shown an aggregate dominated by open-ended documentation work. Report the shape back in the result so a reader cannot mistake which population they are looking at. THE SAMPLE FLOOR IS THE DESIGN, NOT A GUARD. Declare a module-level minimum sample and return, for any lane below it, an explicit insufficient-evidence marker naming the count it has, rather than a figure. State in the docstring that a rate over three rows is not evidence and that publishing one invites a decision the data cannot support; this project has already had a lane comparison rest on five rows across three lanes and a determinism result rest on two measurements that were secretly identical. A surface that refuses is what makes the numbers it does report trustworthy. WHAT TO BUILD AND WHAT NOT TO. Create reckon/crew/lane_evidence.py exposing one function taking the ledger rows, a role and a specification level, and returning the rows described above plus the shape it filtered on. Read rows through the existing ledger reader rather than opening any file yourself. Do NOT register a command-line entry point in this node: reckon/cli.py is held by a peer this hour and a sequenced follow-up owns the command, which is stated here so the absence reads as sequencing rather than oversight. Do not select a lane, rank the rows, or emit a recommendation of any kind: the orchestrator decides and this surface informs, and a module that picks would hide exactly the decision this design exists to expose. Say that in the docstring. Do not touch reckon/crew/dispatch.py, reckon/cli.py, reckon/ledger.py, reckon/crew/quota_weight.py, reckon/crew/rollout.py or reckon/crew/context_budget.py; peers hold all six. FALSIFIERS, in tests/test_lane_evidence.py, every expected figure computed in the test from its own fixture rows rather than written as a literal, and every fixture synthesised rather than read from a real ledger. Two lanes with identical gate outcomes but different rework counts return different rework rates, which is the property gate pass cannot express. A later row re-touching an earlier row's declared write path counts as rework of that earlier row; a retry attempt of the same node does not; a shadow of the same node does not. A row whose manifest said complete and whose promoted classification is work-rejected counts as an overclaim, and a row that blocked and said so does not, asserted side by side so the two failure shapes are provably distinguished. A lane whose rows carry no token quantities reports its cost as unmeasured and NOT as zero, asserted directly against a lane with real quantities so the two cannot compare equal. A lane with fewer rows than the declared floor returns the insufficient-evidence marker carrying its actual count, and a lane at exactly the floor returns figures, so the boundary is pinned in both directions. A caller asking for one role and specification level receives no row derived from any other shape, asserted by including rows of a second shape in the fixture and requiring they contribute nothing to any figure. The returned result names the shape it filtered on. An empty row set returns insufficient evidence for every lane rather than raising or returning an empty success. Measure base and head over the new file and the tests that import reckon.crew, report failure ids either side, require none added, bound the run per file, and never run the full suite for this node.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_quota_weight.py -q passes, and the weight the module returns is proportional to what a run actually consumed rather than to its consumption per token, with the long-context surcharge applied to the tokens inside each crossing request rather than to the whole run. WHY THIS IS A REPAIR AND WHOSE FAULT IT IS. You built exactly what the previous contract specified and eleven tests pass; the contract was wrong in two ways and one of its falsifiers was inverted and passed only because of the first error. Both are the coordinator's, not yours. The module, the declared rate table, the strict family ordering and the explicit refusal for an undeclared model are all correct and land unchanged; only the arithmetic and the signature change. THE FIRST ERROR: THE FIGURE IS AN INTENSITY, NOT A COST. The helper divides the weighted token total by the token total, so a run of sixteen million tokens and a run of six hundred thousand tokens on the same model with the same mix return the SAME weight. A figure that cannot distinguish those two cannot rank anything, and ranking runs by consumption is the only reason this module exists. Return a figure proportional to the run's size: the weighted token total itself, unnormalised, still expressed relative to the reference member's rate so it stays dimensionless and is not a currency amount. Keep the reference member's RATE ratio at one; do not keep any run's weight at one. THE SECOND ERROR: THE SURCHARGE CANNOT BE COMPUTED FROM A COUNT. The published rule charges a request whose input exceeds the threshold at twice input and one and a half times output FOR THAT REQUEST. The current model instead multiplies the whole run's tokens by one plus the crossing count, so two crossings charge three times on every token in the run, including the tokens of requests that never crossed. On a sixteen-million-token run with two crossings that overstates by roughly a factor of three. A crossing count carries no information about how many tokens were inside the crossing requests, so no correct arithmetic can be built from it. CHANGE THE SIGNATURE ACCORDINGLY. Take the model identifier and a sequence of per-request figures, each carrying that request's input tokens and output tokens. Sum the run yourself: for each request, if its input exceeds the threshold apply the surcharge multipliers to that request's own input and output, otherwise apply neither, then weight by the model's rate ratio and add it in. Return the total weight, the rate entry used, the number of requests that crossed, and the token totals with and without the surcharge applied so a caller can see the surcharge's size rather than infer it. Do not accept a bare cumulative total plus a crossing count in any form: the point of the change is that the pair is insufficient, and an optional path taking it would be used. THE PER-REQUEST FIGURES EXIST, so this signature is not a burden on the caller. A peer node landing this hour reads the metered client's own per-session receipt file, whose records carry each request's input and output tokens individually; that is where a caller obtains the sequence. Do not import that module and do not read any file yourself — take plain numbers, so this module stays reviewable on its own — but name that surface in the docstring as the source of the sequence, so a reader knows the signature is satisfiable. FALSIFIERS, in tests/test_quota_weight.py, every expected figure computed in the test from the declared constants rather than written as a literal. Keep every existing test that still holds: the rate ratios for equal quantities, the strict family ordering, the undeclared-model refusal, the known zero, and the negative-input refusal. Delete the inverted comparison test outright and replace it with the correct direction: a run of sixteen million input tokens across many requests none of which crosses weighs STRICTLY MORE than a run of six hundred thousand input tokens across two requests that both cross, because sixteen million tokens at the plain rate exceeds six hundred thousand at twice the rate, and the previous contract asserted the reverse. THE SCALE FALSIFIER, which is the one that catches the normalisation returning: two runs on the same model with the same per-request mix, one exactly ten times the other in request count, return weights whose ratio is ten, asserted against a ratio the test computes. A normalised implementation returns one and fails this. THE PER-REQUEST ATTRIBUTION FALSIFIER: a run of two requests where only one crosses weighs strictly less than a run of the same two requests where both cross, and strictly more than the same two where neither does, with all three figures computed in the test; and the surcharge applied to a run whose crossing request is a small fraction of its tokens changes the total weight by strictly less than the surcharge applied to a run whose crossing request is most of its tokens, which is the property the count-based model could not express at all. An empty request sequence returns a known zero rather than the undeclared-model unknown. A request with a negative token count raises. A request whose input exactly equals the threshold does NOT cross, since the rule is strictly greater, and assert that boundary directly in both directions at the threshold and at the threshold plus one. Measure base and head over the changed file and the tests that import reckon.crew, report failure ids either side, require none added, bound the run per file, and never run the full suite for this node.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_context_budget.py -q passes, and a function in a new module reports, for one run's stream, how many times that run's history was compacted and the largest context size the stream reveals it reached, distinguishing a run that never compacted because it was short from one that never reached the ceiling from one whose stream cannot answer. WHY THIS IS WORTH A NODE. The metered family this fleet dispatches to documents a window near one million tokens while the client ships a much lower tuned default, so until an hour ago every worker here compacted at roughly a third of the model's capability. That default has now been raised in the host configuration. Two things are now unknown and both are decision-relevant. First, whether the raise is honoured at all: published guidance warns that some subscription accounts hit an effective ceiling near 360,000 tokens REGARDLESS of the configured value, and that figure is suspiciously close to the client's own default effective window, so it may describe accounts whose config never took effect rather than a server cap. If our account is capped, a client that believes it has a million tokens will not compact and the request will fail at the server instead, which is worse than compacting. Second, how often we were compacting before, because compaction costs turns and a re-oriented worker re-reads files, and this project has measured that burn is steps multiplied by context. Neither figure exists anywhere today. WHAT THE STREAM MIGHT CARRY, AND YOU MUST DETERMINE IT RATHER THAN ASSUME IT. A peer established this morning that this dialect's streams carry many completed-item records with no usage on them and exactly one aggregate usage record for the whole turn, so per-request token figures are not available. What is NOT yet established is whether the client emits anything when it compacts history, or when it approaches or hits a context ceiling. Find out from real streams under the crew runs directory: there are hundreds, spanning short runs and runs of many hours, and the long ones must have compacted repeatedly under the old default. Search for records whose type or content concerns compaction, context, history, truncation, summarisation or a token limit, and read the actual records rather than matching on a word. If such a record exists it is the most valuable thing in this node, because the context size at the moment of compaction is the ONLY route this dialect offers to a per-request-scale figure, and that figure is what settles the ceiling question. WHAT TO BUILD, IN A NEW MODULE ONLY. Create reckon/crew/context_budget.py exposing one function taking a path to a run's stream and returning the number of compactions observed, the largest context size the stream reveals, the record type each figure was read from, and an explicit unmeasured marker for any figure the stream does not support. Do not wire it into promotion, dispatch, the ledger, the CLI or any surface. Do not read or modify any configuration file. Do not edit reckon/_backends.py, reckon/crew/metering.py, reckon/crew/quota_weight.py, reckon/crew/promotion.py, reckon/crew/prompts.py or docs/research/deploy-matrix.html; peers hold all six this hour. IF THE STREAM CARRIES NO SUCH RECORD, THAT IS THE FINDING AND YOU DELIVER IT. Return the unmeasured marker for both figures on this dialect, state in a comment which record types you searched and how many records of each you examined, and give the count of streams and records you looked at so a later reader can judge the search rather than repeat it. A negative result stated with its search breadth is a real deliverable here; a negative result stated without it is worthless. Do not substitute the aggregate turn usage for a context size — a peer blocked correctly this morning rather than make exactly that substitution, because relabelling a run total as a per-request figure is the defect this work exists to remove. RANGE THE FALSIFIERS OVER THE DOMAIN, NOT OVER THE STREAMS YOU FIND. Every real stream available to you was produced under the OLD configuration, so a test asserting only against real streams ranges over a population in which the new behaviour cannot appear, and this project has shipped a fail-open past a clean suite for exactly that reason. So construct streams for the cases reality cannot yet supply. FALSIFIERS, asserted in tests/test_context_budget.py, every expected figure computed in the test rather than written as a literal. A constructed stream containing three compaction records returns three, and one containing none returns zero rather than the unmeasured marker, so a run that genuinely did not compact is distinguishable from a stream that cannot say. A constructed stream carrying no record of any relevant type returns the unmeasured marker for both figures and does not raise. A missing stream path and an unreadable stream both return the unmeasured marker and do not raise. A constructed stream whose compaction records carry differing context sizes returns the largest, not the first, not the last and not their sum. The largest context size returned is never equal to a cumulative or aggregate total present in the same constructed stream, asserted directly by placing a much larger aggregate figure in the fixture and requiring the returned figure to be the smaller per-compaction one, so the substitution that blocked the peer node cannot pass here either. Run the function over at least twenty real streams of varying length and assert it raises on none of them and returns a coherent result for each, which is a robustness check and not a claim about the figures. Measure base and head over the new file and the tests that import reckon.crew, report failure ids either side, require none added, bound the run per file, and never run the full suite for this node.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_rollout_receipt.py -q passes, and the quota figures the receipt reader returns are keyed by the length of the window they describe rather than by the position they appear in, so a five-hour reading can never be reported as a weekly one. THE DEFECT, measured on this host within the last hour on freshly landed code. reckon/crew/rollout.py reads the rate limit block's primary entry and returns it as the run's quota position. That was written from a sample of one endpoint family, where primary carries the weekly window and secondary is null. A second family on the same account reports the OPPOSITE: primary carries used_percent 94.0 with window_minutes 300, which is five hours, and secondary carries used_percent 42.0 with window_minutes 10080, which is a week. Both entries were present and populated in one record. So the position in the block does not identify the window, and the current reader would publish a nearly exhausted five-hour figure as though it were a weekly one, understating the weekly by more than a factor of two while overstating urgency on the wrong horizon. This is the same shape of defect as a field that means a maximum on one dialect and a sum on another, and it is being reported here rather than discovered later because the code is new. WHAT THE RECORD ACTUALLY CARRIES, verified, so you need not guess: the rate limit block holds limit_id, limit_name, primary, secondary, credits, individual_limit, spend_control_reached, plan_type and rate_limit_reached_type. Each of primary and secondary, when present, holds used_percent, window_minutes and resets_at. Either may be null. WHAT TO CHANGE. Return the quota readings keyed by window length, not by position: read both primary and secondary wherever present, and expose each reading with its own window_minutes, used_percent and reset time, so a caller asks for the window it cares about rather than trusting an ordering. Provide a named accessor for the five-hour horizon and one for the weekly horizon that select by window length, and make each return the explicit unmeasured marker when no entry of that length is present, never the other entry and never a zero. Do not hardcode the two lengths as the only possibilities: select the weekly reading as the entry whose window is a week and the short-horizon reading as the entry whose window is materially shorter, and if the record ever carries a length matching neither, expose it under its own length rather than dropping it, because a silently dropped horizon is how this defect arose. Also return the effective context window already read, and the plan type, both of which vary by family and are decision-relevant: the two families measured here report 258,400 and 121,600 respectively. Keep every existing absence marker and keep a measured zero used_percent as zero. WHAT NOT TO DO. Do not aggregate the two horizons into a single number or a single worst-case figure: they are separate budgets with different reset times and an orchestrator needs both. None of that is written down anywhere an orchestrator reads, and today two peer fleets between them sent five consecutive nodes to one metered lane by omission, maintained rosters whose declarations had no routing authority when they were made, and discovered the working route by reading source. A mechanism nobody knows the rules for is the same defect as a guard that never runs. READ THE PLAN FOR ANYTHING SEMANTIC; DO NOT RESTATE IT. THE ROSTER RE-READ IS THE MOST URGENT PARAGRAPH IN THE FILE: declarations made while the field was decorative now carry routing authority, so a roster built before today steers dispatches it did not steer when it was built, and an orchestrator must list its roster and compare each member's declared harness against the lane it intends before its next wave. Give the command that lists it. THE MEASUREMENT, arriving independently from three sessions across two fleets. One audited 720 ledger rows carrying both a commits list and a manifest commits line: 534 agree, 62 have a ledger list that is a strict SUBSET of the manifest's, and 124 disagree without being a subset. The worst subset case recorded 31 commits as one; another recorded 8 as 1. The 124 are the opposite defect, a worker manifest quoting a revision the coordinator declined in favour of the verified head, so there the presented list resolves and the manifest's does not. A naive mismatch count returns 186 and conflates the two, which would send a reader to the side whose record resolves on two thirds of the hits. THE CONSEQUENCE IS A DISABLED GUARD, NOT MERELY AN UNDER-RECORD. The out-of-scope boundary check runs against the commits a promotion presents, so an incomplete presentation silently switches it off: one reporting session had a scope extension reach the ledger with an empty acceptance list while the same check fired minutes later on a different node over a one-line test helper. WHAT ALREADY EXISTS AND WHY IT DOES NOT COVER THIS. reckon/crew/promotion.py already guards the commitless case: a passing verdict presenting no commits while the worktree head has moved off its base, and it consults the manifest's own commits line first for exactly this reason, with the measured incident recorded in its docstring. But its condition returns early whenever the presented list is non-empty, so a promotion presenting one commit where the manifest declares eight passes through untouched. The absence is caught and the shortfall is not. WHAT TO CHANGE. Extend that guard so a passing promotion whose presented commits are a strict subset of the manifest's declared commits is reported, naming how many were presented, how many the manifest declared, and which revisions are missing. Reuse the existing manifest commits reader rather than adding a second one. It reports and never refuses. The reporting sessions asked for refuse-or-warn and this node implements the warn half only, for a reason their own data supplies: 124 of their 720 rows have the manifest quoting a revision the coordinator declined in favour of one that resolves, so the manifest is not trustworthy enough to gate on, and a refusal keyed on it would block promotions whose presented list resolves at roughly twice the rate it caught incomplete ones. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. Do not alter the existing commitless guard's behaviour or its message. Do not refuse any promotion. Do not treat a manifest revision absent from the repository as authoritative: a manifest may quote a revision that does not resolve, so verify each declared revision resolves in the run's repository before naming it as missing, and say nothing about one that does not resolve rather than reporting it as lost work. Do not report the non-subset case: the coordinator's list is right there and reporting it would name the list that resolves, which is the specific confusion the mismatch count causes. FALSIFIERS, asserted in tests/test_a_short_commit_list_is_reported.py against constructed manifests and a temporary repository. A promotion presenting one of three declared commits is reported, and the report names one, three, and the two missing revisions. A promotion presenting all declared commits is silent. A promotion presenting commits the manifest does not declare is silent, because that case is the coordinator having declined a worker's revision, where the presented list is the one that resolves in the repository. A promotion presenting a superset is silent. A manifest with no commits line at all is silent and does not raise. A declared revision that does not resolve in the repository is not named as missing, asserted with a well-formed forty-character revision that resolves to nothing. The existing commitless guard still fires on a passing promotion with an empty list whose worktree head moved off base, asserted unchanged. Nothing is refused: assert the promotion completes in every case above. Measure base and head over the new file plus every test importing reckon.crew.promotion; report failure ids either side and require none added, and bound the run per file rather than issuing one census.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_the_prompt_carries_the_contract.py -q passes, and a composed dispatch prompt states that the worker commits at each deliverable and writes its manifest before beginning any long output, so the instruction reaches the worker through the channel the worker actually receives. WHY THIS IS THE GAP RATHER THAN A NICETY. reckon carries this discipline in skills/reckon-ship/references/worker-protocol.md, and the composed prompt embeds no protocol reference at all: it is deliberately short and tells the worker to read the plan and section named. So the protocol reaches a worker only if something puts it in the prompt, and nothing does. The consequence was measured across three sessions this week, which independently reported the same class of manifest defect: manifests under-reporting real work, one reading commits pending over a real commit, one reading status complete with its declared artifact absent, three passed runs leaving commits and artifacts blank. One reporting coordinator stated the conclusion as only flight config is enforced, so only flight config is real, and then compensated by hand-writing the discipline into every brief's own done-when text for its next wave. That compensation is the evidence for this node: a coordinator should not have to retype a contract clause into every brief for it to reach a worker. THE DISTINCTION THAT MAKES THIS BELONG IN THE PROMPT RATHER THAN IN A BRIEF. The prompt's own docstring states its principle: anything the live plan already says is omitted, because the worker's first act is to read the plan. That principle is correct and this text does not violate it. Plan content is what THIS node must achieve and varies per node. Contract content is what EVERY node must do regardless of plan, and a worker that never reads the references cannot learn it from anywhere else. Commit-at-each-deliverable is contract content by that test: it is identical for every node reckon will ever dispatch. WHAT TO ADD, AND ITS STATED REASON. Add to the composed prompt that the worker commits each deliverable as it completes rather than once at the end, and writes its manifest carrying whatever it already holds before beginning any long output. State the reason as loss recovery and not as death prevention: a durable write preceding a long generation survives that generation failing. Do not claim it improves the chance of finishing, because that reading was measured and refuted on two fleets independently, one of which found a node that wrote its entire deliverable inside the final six percent of its run and landed cleanly. KEEP IT SHORT, BECAUSE SHORTNESS IS THE PROMPT'S DESIGN AND NOT AN ACCIDENT. The addition is at most four sentences. It names no backend, no model and no lane. It does not restate the manifest path rules, the fence descriptions or the delivery rule, all of which the prompt or the references already carry. WHAT NOT TO CHANGE. Do not add any other protocol text, however useful; a prompt that grows to hold the whole reference stops being read. Do not embed the references by file path or by inclusion, because a path in a prompt is an instruction to go and read, which is the failure this node exists to remove. Do not alter what the prompt says about the plan, the section, the write paths, the peers, the manifest path or the time budget. Do not add a rate limit, a turn limit or a context limit. FALSIFIERS, asserted in tests/test_the_prompt_carries_the_contract.py against a composed prompt built from a constructed node. The composed prompt contains the commit-at-each-deliverable instruction and the manifest-before-long-output instruction. Its stated reason is recovery, and the prompt does not assert that the practice prevents failure or improves completion. The added text is at most four sentences, asserted by counting. No backend, model or lane name appears in the addition. Every other element the prompt carried before is still present, asserted by composing the same node before and after and diffing, so the addition is purely additive. The prompt does not contain a filesystem path to any reference document. A node with no write paths and a node with several both receive the addition, so it is not conditional on shape. Measure base and head over the new file plus every test importing reckon.crew.prompts; report failure ids either side and require none added.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_lanes_view_serving_state.py -q passes, and the lanes view's serving state distinguishes a lane with ample quota, a lane close enough to its ceiling that a dispatch is at risk, and a lane whose reading is too old to support any claim, rather than reporting that a lane will serve at every utilisation below the absolute ceiling. THE DEFECT, measured against the live route minutes after the view landed. reckon/mcp_views.py derives the serving state as exhausted when used percent is at or above one hundred and as will-serve for every other measured value. The utilisation figure is reported in WHOLE NUMBERS, so at-or-above-one-hundred means the lane is completely spent; there is no band between ample and gone. The live reading that exposed it: one endpoint reported ninety-seven percent used and three percent remaining on a three-hundred-minute window, and the view reported that it will serve. By the time that guard can fire, a dispatch has already been refused. This is the same shape as a guard that reports safety it does not provide, and this project has shipped one before: a state that could not fire at any input in its own domain, past a clean gate, because its falsifier ranged over the live inventory rather than over the input range. AND THE READING'S AGE IS IGNORED. That ninety-seven percent observation was fifty-five minutes old when the view served it, on a window that resets in hours, and the row carried the observation time without letting it qualify the claim. A lane's utilisation at some point in the past does not support a statement about whether it will serve now; the older the reading, the less it supports, and a reading old enough supports nothing. The view already carries the observation time on every row, so the input exists and is simply unused. WHAT TO CHANGE. Give the serving state at least three outcomes: one for a lane whose measured utilisation leaves clear room, one for a lane close enough to its ceiling that a dispatch is at risk, and one for a lane whose reading is too old to support a claim about the present. Name them by what the reader should conclude, not by a number. Declare the utilisation band and the staleness horizon as named module constants with a comment giving the reason for each value, and choose values you can justify in that comment rather than round numbers: the utilisation figure is quantised to whole percent, so a band narrower than a few points is measuring quantisation, and the staleness horizon must be short relative to the shortest window the view reports, which is three hundred minutes. Keep the exhausted outcome for a lane at its ceiling. A lane whose reading is stale must not be reported as ample even when the stale figure was low, because that is the direction that costs a refused dispatch; equally it must not be reported as exhausted, because that would hold work for no reason, and the honest third state is what avoids choosing between two wrong answers. FIX THE TWO ABSENCE DEFECTS IN THE SAME NODE, since both are the same error and both were asked for and not delivered. First, a lane that writes no receipt of this kind because it is not metered through this mechanism is a DIFFERENT state from a lane whose receipt should exist and is missing, and the view currently reports both as unreadable with the same reason. Distinguish them: several lanes in the live output are unmetered through this surface by nature and will never have a receipt, and reporting them as unreadable invites a reader to think something is broken. Second, a lane whose receipt is missing carries an observation time anyway, in one live case two days old, which is some other quantity presented in the field a reader will take as the receipt's observation time. When there is no receipt there is no observation, so that field must say so rather than carry a timestamp from elsewhere; if the timestamp is genuinely useful, give it a name that says what it measures. WHAT NOT TO DO. Do not add a recommendation, a ranking, or a preferred lane; the existing test that scans the response for such a field must keep passing, and this node must not weaken it. Do not compute a burn rate or project a reset. Do not change the quota readings themselves, the horizon keying, the effective context window or the plan type. Do not edit reckon/crew/rollout.py, reckon/crew/recovery.py, reckon/crew/ticker.py, reckon/crew/promotion.py, reckon/ledger.py, reckon/crew/quota_weight.py or reckon/schema/flight.yaml; peers hold all seven. Do not edit any file outside the repository, and in particular do not touch the host flight configuration even though it still declares a withdrawn lane; that is the coordinator's to raise. FALSIFIERS, in tests/test_lanes_view_serving_state.py, every fixture synthesised, no test reading the real configuration home or a real session file, and every expected figure computed in the test from the declared constants rather than written as a literal. RANGE THE UTILISATION FALSIFIER OVER THE INPUT RANGE, NOT OVER THE LANES THAT HAPPEN TO EXIST: assert the state at a sweep of utilisation values from zero to one hundred inclusive, including every value in the at-risk band and the values immediately either side of its boundary, and require the boundary to fall exactly where the constant declares. A fixture at ninety-seven percent on a fresh reading does NOT report the ample state, asserted directly against the ample state's own value, which is the live case that exposed this. A fixture at the ceiling still reports exhausted. A fixture whose reading is older than the staleness horizon reports the stale state regardless of how low its utilisation is, asserted with a deliberately low utilisation so a lenient implementation cannot pass. A fixture one second inside the horizon reports on its utilisation, pinning the boundary both ways. A lane unmetered through this surface reports its own state, distinguishable from a lane whose receipt is missing, asserted against each other directly. A lane with no receipt reports no observation time rather than a timestamp, asserted by requiring the field to be the unmeasured marker. Every existing lanes-view test passes unchanged. Report base and head over tests/test_lanes_view_serving_state.py, tests/test_crew_lanes_view.py and the tests importing reckon.mcp_views, with failure ids either side and none added. Bound the run per file and never run the full suite.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_promotion_harvests_the_receipt.py -q passes, and promoting a run on a metered lane attaches that lane's quota reading, harvested by the harness from the client's own per-session receipt, to both the promotion result the orchestrator reads and the committed ledger row, marking an unmetered or unreadable lane as unmeasured rather than as zero. WHY THIS SHAPE AND NOT A POLL. An orchestrator needs to know which lanes will serve its next dispatch. A poll has to guess when to look and is stale the moment it returns. A terminal run already holds a first-party reading of exactly the lane it just consumed, taken at the instant it stopped consuming it, and the orchestrator is already reading at that moment because promotion is a beat it cannot skip. So the freshest available reading rides along at no extra call. Two consequences beyond convenience. The quota field is reported in whole numbers, so no single reading can attribute one run's cost, but every terminal run stamps one reading with its own observation time, and many readings across a day recover a per-lane burn rate that no individual reading could; today's fleet would already have produced about twenty. And the availability surface being built alongside this can then read the most recent terminal reading per lane and say how old it is, instead of hunting session files. THE HARNESS HARVESTS IT; THE WORKER MUST NOT REPORT IT. This is the load-bearing constraint and it is not negotiable. Read the receipt in the promotion code path, from the client's own file, keyed by the run's recorded session id. Do not add a manifest field for it, do not read it from anything the worker wrote, and do not ask a worker for it. A metric a worker states about its own run stops being independent evidence of that run: this project has measured a brief that merely named a signature contaminating every stream in a wave and the verification along with it. State that reason in a comment at the harvest site, because the next reader will otherwise think a manifest field would have been simpler. WHERE TO GET IT. Read through reckon.crew.rollout, which already locates a session's receipt by its session id and already returns quota readings keyed by the length of the window they describe, with a weekly accessor and a short-horizon accessor. Attach every horizon the receipt reports, each with its window length, its utilisation, its reset time and the time the reading was observed. Do not select one horizon and do not reduce them to a worst case: they are separate budgets with different reset times, measured four hours apart on one account today, and an orchestrator needs each. Also attach the effective context window the receipt reports, which varies by lane by a factor of two and is the best single predictor of whether a node fits. THREE STATES THAT MUST NOT COLLAPSE. A lane that reports no quota because it is unmetered, a lane whose receipt could not be read, and a lane whose window genuinely reads zero used are three different facts. Mark the first two unmeasured, each distinguishably, and keep a measured zero as zero. This project already nulls and flags an unmetered lane's cost rather than recording it as free, precisely so a free lane cannot rank as the cheapest on a surface that sorts by cost; follow that precedent rather than inventing a second convention. WHAT NOT TO DO. Do not make promotion fail, refuse or warn because a receipt is missing: promotion's job is unchanged and an absent reading is a normal outcome for an unmetered lane. Do not compute headroom, a verdict, an availability judgement or a burn rate here; this attaches a reading. Do not touch reckon/crew/quota_weight.py, reckon/_flight_schema.py, reckon/_mcp_tools.py, reckon/mcp_views.py, reckon/mcp.py or reckon/crew/rollout.py; peers hold the first two and the middle three, and the last is the module you consume rather than change. Add the new record key to the ledger's declared record fields, since a tuple there is now held complete by a test and a key written without being declared is the drift that test exists to catch. FALSIFIERS, in tests/test_promotion_harvests_the_receipt.py, using the project's existing promotion test fixtures and a synthesised temporary repository, never a real checkout and never the real configuration home or live-pointer directory. A promotion of a run whose fixture receipt reports two horizons attaches both, each identifiable by its window length, and the shorter horizon's utilisation never appears as the longer one's, asserted against the longer one's value directly. The attached reading appears on BOTH the promotion result and the committed ledger row, asserted separately, because one without the other is the half-delivery this project has repeatedly measured: a capability that lands in the module owning the mechanism while the surface a reader reaches stays unchanged. A promotion of a run on a lane whose fixture declares it unmetered attaches an unmeasured marker and not a zero, asserted against a fixture whose measured utilisation is genuinely zero so the two cannot compare equal. A promotion whose receipt is absent attaches the unmeasured marker, distinguishably from the unmetered case, and the promotion still succeeds with its existing result unchanged in every other respect. The attached reading carries an observation time. Every existing promotion test passes with its assertions unchanged, which is the pin on promotion's unchanged behaviour, and the record-field completeness test passes with the new key declared. Report base and head over tests/test_promotion_harvests_the_receipt.py, the existing promotion tests, and the record-field completeness test, with failure ids either side and none added. Bound the run per file and never run the full suite.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_quota_weight.py -q passes, tests/test_skill_contracts.py reports no failure attributable to reckon/crew/quota_weight.py, and that module names no concrete model identifier and encodes no relative ordering between named models; the rates it applies arrive from configuration instead. THE VIOLATION, and it is the coordinator's doing. reckon/crew/quota_weight.py lines 17 to 19 declare three module constants binding a concrete model identifier each, and their names encode a hierarchy between them: one is the reference, one the middle, one the efficient member. A repository contract test fails on this, and the binding rule behind that test is that source, plans, skills and schemas may record task requirements and validation floors but must not prescribe concrete models, model families, or relative model hierarchies. A worker on an unrelated documentation node found the red test, correctly declined to fix it outside its scope, and reported it. The earlier brief for that module asked for exactly this shape, so the module did what it was told and the contract is what was wrong with the instruction. WHY THE RULE IS RIGHT HERE AND NOT MERELY A LINT. Two independent reasons, both of which this module already violates in substance. A rate is a moving number, and a moving number written into source is a fuse: when the vendor reprices, the module lies with no code change and no test failure. And a hierarchy in source makes the code the authority on which lane is stronger, which is a policy question the operator owns and which the surrounding design has deliberately refused to answer anywhere else — every other component built today reports and declines to rank. WHAT TO CHANGE. Take the rate table from the project's flight configuration through the existing flight reader rather than from module constants, so a lane's rate lives beside that lane's other declarations and a repricing is a configuration edit. Read the rates for the backends configuration declares; where a backend declares no rate, that backend must return the existing explicit unknown, which is the behaviour the module already has for an unrecognised identifier and which must be preserved exactly. Remove the three constants and every name that encodes a position in a hierarchy. Choose a reference for the dimensionless ratio without naming a model in source: derive it from the configuration itself, and state in a comment how the reference is chosen and why the choice cannot be a model name. If the configuration declares no rates at all, every lookup returns the unknown and nothing raises; a module that cannot price anything must say so rather than fall back to a table. ADD THE RATES TO CONFIGURATION AS PART OF THIS NODE, in the flight configuration schema and its declared defaults inside the repository, never in any file outside it: you must not edit anything under the user's home configuration directory. Put the per-million input and output rates alongside each backend's existing declaration in the repository's own schema and example or default configuration, so the shape is documented where a reader configuring a lane will meet it. The three rates currently in the module are the ones to carry across; take them from the module as it stands rather than from any other source, because preserving today's numbers exactly is what makes this a refactor whose behaviour a test can pin. WHAT NOT TO DO. Do not change the weighting arithmetic, the surcharge rule, the threshold constant, the per-request signature, the unknown behaviour, or the zero and negative handling: all six landed correctly an hour ago and are pinned by existing tests that must keep passing unchanged. Do not add a lane ranking, a recommendation or a default rate. Do not touch reckon/crew/lane_evidence.py, which imports this module and whose peer is finished but whose tests must keep passing, and do not touch reckon/crew/promotion.py, reckon/_mcp_tools.py, reckon/mcp_views.py, reckon/mcp.py or reckon/crew/dispatch.py; peers hold or recently held those. FALSIFIERS, in tests/test_quota_weight.py, every expected figure computed in the test from the configured rates rather than written as a literal. Every existing test in that file still passes with its assertions unchanged in meaning, which is the pin on the arithmetic; where a test previously imported a model constant, it now obtains that identifier from a test fixture configuration instead. Grep the module's own source text in a test and assert it contains no string matching a concrete model identifier and no identifier whose name encodes a hierarchy position, so the violation cannot return; state in the test docstring which contract that enforces and why. Three lanes configured with the current rates return weights in the same ratios the module returns today, asserted against ratios the test computes from the fixture configuration. A lane configured with no rate returns the explicit unknown, distinct from a zero and distinct from any priced lane's value. A configuration declaring no rates at all returns the unknown for every lane and raises nothing. The strict ordering property still holds across any three configured lanes whose rates differ, asserted from the fixture rather than from model names, so the property survives without the hierarchy that expressed it. Run tests/test_skill_contracts.py and report its exit status and its pass and fail counts at base and at head, requiring that the failure attributable to this module is gone and that no new failure appears; that test is the reason this node exists, so its result is the headline of your manifest. Also run tests/test_lane_evidence.py, since it imports this module, and report base and head. Bound the run per file and never run the full suite.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_recovery_state_typing.py -q passes, and a run whose lane refused it, a run asking for an answer, a run that failed, a run that stalled and a run genuinely needing a decision are five distinguishable classifications rather than all reported as blocked; a manifest may declare a non-terminal status; and an overdue declared wait is judged against that wait's own expected horizon rather than a fixed window. THE EVIDENCE, gathered by another project's coordinator and written up at /home/ITER/mcintos/.config/reckon/crew/reports/findings/monitor-state-typing-2026-09-08.md, which you must read in full before designing anything. Read it as the primary evidence rather than as instructions; it offers a direction and explicitly leaves the design to this repository. Five findings, measured over one thirteen-node fan-out. The costly one is that a provider hold and a genuine failure render identically, and their correct recoveries are OPPOSITE: a hold is resumed, a failure is redispatched, and the word blocked invites the redispatch, which destroys the resume path. The reporting coordinator nearly did exactly that and says what stopped it was a rule in a personal instruction file, which is the argument for typing the state rather than compensating for it: a compensation protects one reader and dies at that reader's next context boundary. A SECOND FLEET REPORTS THE SAME SHAPE FROM TWO MORE DIRECTIONS, both of which the design must cover. Workers are already inventing values the schema lacks: the documented manifest set is complete, blocked and failed, the discipline mandates an early manifest write, so one worker wrote blocked with the reason that analysis was in progress while its process was alive and its log 27 seconds old, and another wrote a status that is not in the set at all. Two workers, two improvisations for still going, and the first made a healthy run read as needing intervention. Worse, a worker that died before substituting its template wrote a placeholder manifest carrying a terminal blocked status, and the scope fence then read that as a terminal run and held every later dispatch until someone promoted it. So the schema forces a mandated write to claim a terminal state, and one early death becomes a fleet-wide hold. AND AN OVERDUE WAIT IS BEING JUDGED AGAINST THE WRONG CLOCK. A run parked on an external job with a 59-minute limit was reported wait-aged after 900 seconds, which reads as an alarm for a wait that is exactly on schedule. A declared wait carries its own expectation; the age that matters is age against that expectation, not against a constant. WHAT TO DESIGN, and the shape is yours within these constraints. Put the cause in the classification rather than only in a prose detail, so a reader acting on the type alone acts correctly. At minimum separate a lane refusal or quota hold, whose recovery is to wait or move lane and never to redispatch, and which must carry a reset time when one is known and say plainly when it is not; a run asking for an answer, whose recovery is to answer and resume; a failure, whose recovery is a corrective dispatch; a stall, whose recovery is to investigate; and a genuine blocked, meaning a decision is needed. Carry the recovery verb in the row: one existing surface already does this well, reporting a resume command with the condition that lifts it, and the follower line omits exactly that. Make one field authoritative for what the coordinator should do now, and either leave the advisory field advisory or reconcile it against liveness before rendering, because four fields telling four stories about one run was measured. Give the manifest a non-terminal status so a mandated early write need not claim a terminal state, and make an unsubstituted template manifest read as unwritten rather than as terminal. Judge an overdue declared wait against the horizon that wait declares. PRESERVE WHAT ALREADY WORKS, and it is written into the module: the existing comment distinguishing the stop that lifts itself from the stop that demands a reader is the correct principle and your vocabulary must keep it, including the requirement that a self-lifting state always names what will lift it so it never becomes the bucket a forgotten run sits in. Keep every existing classification that still means something and do not rename one whose meaning you are not changing. WHAT NOT TO DO. Do not change the resume gate's budget reading in this node: that is the reported finding about two surfaces disagreeing at one instant, it needs the lane probe, and it is a separate node. Do not touch reckon/crew/promotion.py, reckon/ledger.py, reckon/crew/quota_weight.py, reckon/crew/lane_evidence.py, reckon/_mcp_tools.py, reckon/mcp_views.py, reckon/mcp.py, reckon/schema/flight.yaml or reckon/crew/dispatch.py; peers hold or recently held all nine. Do not add a state whose recovery is the same as an existing state's; a distinction that changes no action is noise. FALSIFIERS, in tests/test_recovery_state_typing.py, every fixture synthesised and never reading the real configuration home or live-pointer directory. A fixture run refused by its lane classifies distinguishably from a fixture run that failed, asserted directly against each other, and the refused one's recovery text names resuming while the failed one's does not name resuming, so the two opposite recoveries cannot be confused by a reader following the type. A refused run with a known reset time carries it; one without says so explicitly rather than omitting the field. A fixture manifest declaring a non-terminal status with a live process and a fresh log does NOT classify as blocked, which is the healthy-run-reads-as-actionable case. A template manifest whose placeholders are unsubstituted classifies as unwritten and NOT as terminal, and a test asserts it does not satisfy whatever predicate the scope fence uses for terminality, so one early death cannot hold a fleet. A declared wait with a long horizon is not overdue at an age that would be overdue for a short one, asserted by two fixtures differing only in their declared horizon, which is the property a fixed window cannot express. Every row carrying an actionable classification also carries a recovery verb, asserted over the whole vocabulary by iterating it rather than by naming states one at a time, so a future state cannot be added without one. The self-lifting states each name what lifts them, asserted the same way. Every existing recovery test passes with its assertions unchanged in meaning. Report base and head over tests/test_recovery_state_typing.py, the existing recovery and ticker tests, and the crew tests, with failure ids either side and none added. Bound the run per file and never run the full suite.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_lane_change_reads_the_worktree.py -q passes, and the prompt a redispatched worker receives states the inherited worktree's actual state, read at the moment the prompt is composed rather than described by the coordinator from an earlier reading. THE DEFECT AND THE MEASURED COST, reported by another fleet's coordinator today. reckon/crew/dispatch.py composes the fresh-start prompt in _lane_prompt around line 3063: it reads the original prompt from disk, appends a lane-changed notice, the reason and the coordinator's advice, and stops. Nothing in it reads the worktree the new worker is about to inherit. So the only account of that worktree is whatever the coordinator wrote into the advice, from a reading taken before the outgoing worker was stopped. Measured: a coordinator's advice said the inherited worktree carried no modifications, the outgoing worker made its first and only edit, a single import line, in the seconds between that reading and the stop, and the incoming worker refused to start on an unexpected pre-existing modification to an assigned path. The handoff went stale inside the window the procedure itself creates, and no amount of coordinator care closes that window, because the reading and the stop cannot be simultaneous. A SECOND MEASURED CASE MAKES THE SAME POINT FROM THE OTHER SIDE, and it is the more expensive one. A worker was killed at its harness ceiling while an external compute job it had submitted kept running; the recoverable fact was a live job owned by a dead run, and it existed only as prose in the dead worker's manifest. A redispatch onto another lane recovered it, but only because the coordinator happened to put the job id into the advice by hand. The general shape of both cases is the same: the successor is told about its inheritance by a human intermediary rather than by a reading, and everything the intermediary omits or misremembers is lost. WHAT TO CHANGE. When composing a fresh-start prompt for a lane change, read the inherited worktree at that moment and state what is there: the porcelain status and a per-file change summary, and the head commit the worktree sits on together with whether that commit differs from the run's recorded base. Put it in the prompt as a stated fact rather than as advice, clearly separated from the coordinator's own advice so the worker can tell a reading from an instruction, and label it with the time it was taken. Keep the coordinator's advice exactly as it is passed; this adds a reading, it does not replace or edit what the coordinator wrote. When the porcelain status returns no entries, say that explicitly rather than omitting the section, because an absent section is indistinguishable from a section nobody generated. ALSO SURFACE THE UNCOMMITTED WORK AS THE EXPOSURE IT IS. Where the reading shows uncommitted changes, the prompt must instruct the successor to commit them as a checkpoint before continuing, and say why in one clause: an inherited diff is the only copy of that work and a later refusal or death takes it. That instruction has been given by hand by two coordinators today and worked both times; putting it in the composed prompt is what stops it depending on either of them remembering. WHAT NOT TO DO. Do not read or run anything outside the inherited worktree, and do not attempt to discover external compute jobs in this node; the abandoned-run job-recovery case belongs to a separate node in the classification module, which a peer holds. Do not change the same-session advice path, which passes the coordinator's advice through unchanged and must keep doing so. Do not change what the lane change does to the run record, the backend resolution, or the retained worktree itself. Do not edit reckon/crew/recovery.py, reckon/crew/ticker.py, reckon/mcp_views.py, reckon/crew/quota_weight.py, reckon/schema/flight.yaml or reckon/ledger.py; peers hold all six. Do not fail a lane change because the worktree cannot be read: state that it could not be read, and why, and continue, because refusing to hand off a run whose worktree is unreadable strands it exactly where the old behaviour stranded it. FALSIFIERS, in tests/test_lane_change_reads_the_worktree.py, using a synthesised temporary git repository as the inherited worktree, never a real checkout and never the real configuration home. A fresh-start prompt composed against a worktree carrying an uncommitted modification contains that file's path, and contains the checkpoint instruction; assert both, and assert the path appears even when the coordinator's advice is empty, which is the case the coordinator cannot cover by hand. A prompt composed against a worktree whose porcelain status returns no entries contains an affirmative statement to that effect, asserted by looking for that statement rather than by asserting the absence of a path. node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_lanes_view_is_live.py -q passes, and the lanes view never reports a quota reading as too old to use: it obtains a live reading by probing, and where a probe cannot describe a particular lane's own quota it falls back to that lane's own most recent receipt and names which source answered. WHY THE CURRENT BEHAVIOUR IS WRONG. The view was given a stale state an hour ago because its only input was a per-session receipt file that ages, and reporting an old reading as current would have been worse. That was the right call for the inputs it had and the wrong design for the tool: this surface exists so an orchestrator can ask whether a lane will serve before dispatching, and answering that it does not know is a refusal to do its one job when the means to answer exist. A live probe exists in this repository and the view does not use it. WHAT THE PROBE IS, so you do not have to find it. reckon/_backends.py defines budget_probe for the metered dialect: it launches the harness command's app-server transport and issues an initialize handshake followed by an account rate-limits read, and that read RUNS NO MODEL, so it costs no quota and no tokens. Its answer carries used percentages and reset times for SEVERAL metered windows at once. read_probe currently reduces that answer to a single window, choosing whichever is furthest through. The probe machinery, its caching field and a cache lifetime in the budget policy all already exist; what is missing is the lanes view consulting it. THE ROOT DEFECT THE PROBE ALONE DOES NOT FIX, and this is the part to get right. The probe is keyed to the harness COMMAND, and four configured lanes share one command, so a single account reading is currently attributed to four lanes whose quotas differ. Measured on this host: the budget surface reports all four at an identical utilisation and an identical burn multiple, while one of those lanes has its own separate quota entirely, sitting at 97 percent of a five-hour window and 43 percent of a weekly window that resets about 3.7 hours later than the shared one. So a probe used naively would still describe that lane with another lane's figure, and it would do so with the authority of a fresh reading, which is worse than a stale one. WHAT TO BUILD. Probe for a live reading when composing the view. Key every window the probe returns by its own window_minutes rather than reducing to one, the way the receipt reader already does, and expose each. For every lane, decide which source describes THAT lane and say so on the row: a probe reading whose windows match the lane's own quota structure, or that lane's own most recent receipt where the probe cannot distinguish it. Carry the source name and the observation time on every reading, so a reader can see whether it came from a live probe or from a receipt, and never present a receipt figure as a probe reading. Keep the at-risk band and the exhausted state exactly as they are. Retire the stale state ONLY for lanes the probe can describe; a lane whose only available evidence is an old receipt must still say so rather than pretend, because inventing currency is the failure this whole surface exists to prevent — the honest form is a fresh-probe row for lanes the probe covers and a receipt-sourced row, with its age, for lanes it does not.
