node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_promotion_beat_carries_fleet_state.py -q passes, and the result a promotion returns carries a short fleet-state reading beside the quota reading it already carries, so an orchestrator's picture of its own fleet is refreshed at every landing without a separate read. WHY THIS COMPLETES A HALF-BUILT DESIGN. Promotion already attaches a lane quota reading harvested from the client's own receipt, and that half works: the newest promoted row carries quota_state, an observation time, the effective context window and the quota windows keyed by length. What it does not carry is anything about the FLEET, and the fleet is what the orchestrator is about to make its next decision about. So a coordinator that has just landed a node still has to issue a separate read to learn whether anything else is live, whether a run is unreconciled, whether a lane is occupied, or whether a followup is waiting — at exactly the moment it is already reading a result. The promotion beat is the one moment an orchestrator cannot skip, which is why the reading belongs there rather than on a schedule. WHAT TO ATTACH, and the constraint that matters most is BREVITY. This is a beat, not a report: a handful of scalars an orchestrator can act on without parsing. Include the number of runs still live in this project, the number that are unreconciled, the count of runs whose classification is actionable together with the classifications present, and the number of distinct lanes currently occupied. Include the fleet observation time. Do not attach per-run rows, worktree paths, manifest digests, follower registrations or anything that grows with fleet size: a beat that grows unboundedly stops being read, and every one of those is already available from the views that exist for them. If you find yourself attaching a list whose length is the number of runs, stop and attach its count instead. DERIVE IT, DO NOT RECOMPUTE IT. The counts above are already derived by the existing live-pointer and drain reads; call those rather than reimplementing their logic, so the beat and the views cannot drift into disagreeing about one fleet. That is the whole point of putting the derivation in one place, and a second implementation of a count is the defect this project has repeatedly measured. THREE RULES. The beat is a reading and carries its own observation time, separate from the quota reading's, because the two are taken from different sources and one being fresh says nothing about the other. The beat never fails a promotion: if the fleet state cannot be read, attach an explicit unmeasured marker saying so and let the promotion succeed unchanged, exactly as the quota reading already degrades. And the beat states facts and recommends nothing: no readiness verdict, no next-node suggestion, no capacity judgement, because the orchestrator owns that decision and every other surface built here refuses to make it. Say that in a comment at the composition site. WHAT NOT TO TOUCH. Do not change what promotion does to the run record, the gate, the commit list, the suite delta or the lane quota receipt. Do not add the beat to the ledger row: the ledger is a durable record of one run and a fleet snapshot at that moment does not describe that run, so this belongs on the returned RESULT only, and a test must assert the ledger row is unchanged by it. Do not edit reckon/mcp_views.py, reckon/_backends.py, reckon/crew/recovery.py, reckon/crew/ticker.py or reckon/crew/rollout.py; a peer holds the first two and the rest are settled. FALSIFIERS, in tests/test_promotion_beat_carries_fleet_state.py, using the project's existing promotion fixtures and a synthesised temporary repository, never a real checkout and never the real configuration home or live-pointer directory. A promotion whose fixture fleet holds several live runs returns a beat whose live count equals the number the test constructed, and the same for the unreconciled count and the occupied-lane count, each asserted against a figure the test computes rather than a literal. The beat carries its own observation time, distinct from the quota reading's, asserted by constructing the two at different times and requiring both to appear. THE BEAT IS BOUNDED: assert that its size does not grow with fleet size, by composing it against a fixture with one live run and against one with many and requiring the same set of keys and no list whose length differs; that is the assertion that keeps it a beat. A fixture whose fleet state cannot be read yields the unmeasured marker and a promotion that still succeeds with its other fields unchanged. The committed ledger row is byte-identical with and without the beat, asserted directly, so the durable record is untouched. The beat contains no field naming a recommended, preferred, ready or suggested next action, asserted by scanning its keys and values, pinning the no-recommendation rule the way the lanes view already pins it. Every existing promotion test passes with its assertions unchanged. Report base and head over the new file and the existing promotion tests, with failure ids either side and none added. Bound the run per file and never run the full suite.

node_definition.done_when: A report file exists at the declared write path stating whether this worker could call the imas-dd MCP server from inside its own dispatched process, naming the tool it called, the version range that tool returned, and the verbatim error if it could not. WHY THIS IS WORTH A NODE AND WHY YOU ARE THE RIGHT PROCESS TO RUN IT. Dispatch here is command-line led: the coordinator launches a separate harness process, so whatever tools THAT harness has are what a worker has, and they are not the coordinator's tools. The coordinator can call an MCP server and learn nothing about you. Only a call made inside your own process settles it. The host configuration declares three MCP servers to your harness — one served over HTTP at an ITER address, one launched as a local module, one launched through a project runner — and nobody has ever confirmed that a non-interactive dispatched run reaches any of them. If it does, briefs across this fleet can start naming authoritative lookups instead of asking workers to infer facts. If it does not, that is equally valuable and must be recorded as plainly. WHAT TO DO. Attempt to call the imas-dd MCP server for the range of IMAS data-dictionary versions it knows about — the earliest and the latest, and however it expresses the set between them. Use whatever tool that server exposes for listing or describing versions; discover the tool from the server rather than assuming a name, and record the exact tool name you called. Then write the report. THE REPORT MUST DISTINGUISH FOUR OUTCOMES, and stating which one occurred is the deliverable. The server answered and you have a version range. The server was reachable but the call was refused or errored, in which case give the verbatim error. The tools were not present in your process at all, meaning the harness exposed no MCP surface to this run. Or the attempt could not be made for some other reason you name. Do not collapse any of these into another, and do not report an inability as a version range. THE ANTI-FABRICATION RULE IS THE POINT OF THE WHOLE NODE. You may know something about IMAS data-dictionary versions from training, and a plausible answer from memory would be indistinguishable in the report from a real tool result while being worthless as evidence about tool access. So the report must carry, for the successful case, the tool name you called and the response as the tool returned it, and must state explicitly that the figures came from that call. If you cannot call a tool, you must NOT supply a version range from any other source — not from memory, not from a file on disk, not from a web page. Say the call failed and give the error. A report containing a version range without a tool name and a tool response is a failed node regardless of whether the numbers are correct. Do not read any repository file, environment variable or configuration file to answer the version question: the question is whether the TOOL answers, and any other route defeats it. WHAT ELSE TO RECORD, because it costs you nothing and answers the next question. List every MCP tool name visible in your process, if any are, so the fleet learns what a dispatched worker actually has rather than what the configuration declares. If the list is empty, say so as a list of length zero rather than as prose. Note whether any call required an approval you could not give, since one server is configured with an approval mode and a non-interactive process cannot answer a prompt — that specific outcome, a tool present but unusable without an approver, is the one most likely to be misread as absence, so name it if you meet it. WHAT NOT TO DO. Write nothing outside the declared write path. Do not install, start, configure or edit any MCP server, and do not edit any configuration file. Do not attempt to work around a failure by calling the server over plain HTTP yourself: the question is what the harness gives you, and a manual request answers a different one. Do not run the repository's test suite; this node has no code gate. FALSIFIERS. The report exists at the declared path and names exactly one of the four outcomes. For the successful case it carries the tool name, the tool's own response, and the earliest and latest versions read from that response. For any unsuccessful case it carries the verbatim error text or the empty tool list. The report states the harness and model it was produced by, taken from your own runtime rather than from the brief, so a later reader can tell which lane was tested. The report contains no version figure that is not attributable to a named tool response, which you confirm by rereading your own report before finishing and saying in the manifest that you did. State in the manifest the count of MCP tools you could see.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_mcp_tool_names_are_regular.py -q passes, and every tool the reckon MCP server publishes carries an explicit wire name with no leading underscore, so each is addressed as mcp followed by the server name, a double separator, and the tool name, exactly as the other servers on this workstation are. THE DEFECT, measured from inside two dispatched worker processes today. The server registers five tools with a FastMCP decorator applied to module-private functions named with a leading underscore, and FastMCP takes the wire name from the function name. So the underscore that marks a function private in Python leaks into the published name and absorbs a separator. Measured: three of the four MCP servers declared on this workstation publish as mcp, server, double separator, tool. Reckon alone publishes with a single separator on one host and with three underscores on another, for the same five tools. That is not cosmetic. A coordinator matching tool names by pattern found none of reckon's tools, concluded the server was unreachable from dispatched workers, reported that as a finding, and was wrong; the server was answering the whole time. The irregularity cost a false absence claim in a committed record. WHAT TO CHANGE. Give each of the five tool registrations an explicit published name equal to the function name with its leading underscore removed, so the five become the plain nouns and verbs they already are. Keep every Python function name exactly as it is: those underscores are correct, the functions are module-private, and renaming them would ripple through internal call sites for no benefit. The change is confined to the decorator call. Read the file to find all five rather than trusting a list, and say in your manifest how many you found, because a rename that misses one leaves the inconsistency it exists to remove. UPDATE THE HOST HARNESS CONFIGURATION IN THE SAME NODE, because two of the five are named there and would otherwise silently stop matching. The workstation configuration file for the metered harness declares per-tool approval settings keyed by the old names for two of these tools. Those keys must move to the new names. That file is outside the repository; you are permitted to edit ONLY those two keys in it and nothing else, and you must report the before and after of each line you touched verbatim in your manifest. Do not add, remove or reorder any other key, and do not touch any other file outside the repository. THIS IS A BREAKING CHANGE AND MUST BE STATED WHERE A CALLER WILL MEET IT. Any session holding a connection to this server keeps calling the old names until it reconnects, and will meet a tool-not-found. Record the old and new spelling for both host conventions in the repository's own documentation of this surface, so the next reader can map a stale call rather than guess. Find where this server's tools are already documented and put it there rather than creating a new file. WHAT NOT TO DO. Do not change any tool's arguments, behaviour, return shape or description. Do not add or remove a tool. Do not change the server's own name. Do not touch reckon/crew/recovery.py, reckon/mcp_views.py, reckon/crew/promotion.py or reckon/_backends.py. Do not restart or reconnect anything: the operator owns that beat and a worker cannot do it. FALSIFIERS, in tests/test_mcp_tool_names_are_regular.py. Instantiate or introspect the server and assert the published name of every registered tool, by iterating the registry rather than by naming the five, so a sixth tool added later is held to the same rule. Assert no published name begins with an underscore. Assert every published name matches the same shape as the others, stated as a pattern in the test with the contract named in its docstring. Assert the count of registered tools is unchanged from before your edit, computed in the test rather than written as a literal, so the rename cannot have dropped or added one. Assert each of the five publishes the exact expected plain name, derived in the test from the function names by stripping one leading underscore rather than hard-coded, so the test states the rule instead of restating the answer. Assert the Python function names still carry their leading underscore, which pins that only the wire name moved. And read the host configuration file back and assert the two approval keys carry the new names and that the file still parses, without asserting anything else about its contents. Report base and head over the new file and every test importing reckon.mcp, with failure ids either side and none added. Bound the run per file and never run the full suite.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_a_brief_points_rather_than_quotes.py -q passes, and a dispatch whose done-when reproduces a long contiguous span of its own plan section's text is reported at dispatch time with that span quoted back, so a coordinator sees it has copied the plan instead of pointing at it. WHY A CHECK AND NOT MORE GUIDANCE. The rule already exists, in writing, in this repository: skills/reckon-ship/references/sprint-orchestration.md says do not restate plan context, decisions, research or done-when criteria in the dispatch. Two coordinators broke it seven times between them today, and every one produced a defect. Mine, four: a done-when naming a discriminator the plan had already rejected, so the worker faced two contradictory authorities and changed nothing; a fence naming a generated file as the place to declare a configuration field; a fence excluding the test that imports the symbol the node had to remove; and an instruction to put values in a configuration layer whose own invariant forbids them. A peer's, three: a test list naming a file that exists only in a held prototype tree, an environment variable the production function does not honour, and a receipt path that had been re-keyed out from under the brief. In all seven the worker blocked or disputed and the change it named was the one that landed, while the coordinator's copy named a file, variable, path or measure that the source did not carry. So a written rule with no check decays exactly as this project has recorded elsewhere, and the remedy is a check bound to the moment that always happens. WHAT TO BUILD. At dispatch, after the node's plan and section are resolved and before the worker is launched, compare the done-when text against the text of that plan section. Where a contiguous run of the plan's own words reappears in the done-when beyond a declared length, report it: name the overlapping span, quote it, and say which plan section it came from. Put the report on the dispatch result so a coordinator reading the launch sees it, and record it on the run so a later reader can find it. Declare the length threshold as a named module constant with a comment justifying its value; choose it from what discriminates rather than from a round number, and say in the comment what a shorter span would catch that is legitimate. REPORT, DO NOT REFUSE, AND SAY WHY IN A COMMENT. A done-when legitimately shares short phrases with its plan: a file path, a function name, a measure's units, a threshold figure. Those are pointers, which is the behaviour the rule wants, and a refusal on them would make the check hated and then disabled. A long verbatim paragraph is a copy. The check therefore reports rather than blocks, and the report is the deliverable: a coordinator who sees its own copied paragraph quoted back will fix the brief, and one who is told a number is over a threshold will not. Do not add a flag to suppress it, and do not make it configurable off. NORMALISE BEFORE COMPARING, or the check is trivially defeated and worthless. The plan is HTML and the done-when is prose, so strip markup, collapse whitespace and compare on words rather than characters; a coordinator who reflows a copied paragraph has still copied it. Do not compare on a digest of the whole text, which changes with one word. Do not use a similarity score: a percentage cannot be quoted back to a reader, and quoting the span is the entire point. WHAT NOT TO TOUCH. Do not edit reckon/mcp.py, tests under it, or docs/AGENTS.md; a peer holds all three. Do not change the eight-property node contract, the existing dispatchability refusals, or any other validation. Do not read a plan from anywhere except the resolved plan the node already names, and do not fetch anything. FALSIFIERS, in tests/test_a_brief_points_rather_than_quotes.py, using the project's existing dispatch fixtures and a synthesised temporary repository, never a real checkout and never the real configuration home. A done-when carrying a long verbatim paragraph from its plan section produces a report naming the section and quoting the overlapping span, asserted by finding the span text inside the report rather than by asserting a boolean. RANGE THE FALSIFIER OVER SPAN LENGTH, which is the dimension the threshold lives on: assert the outcome at a sweep of overlap lengths either side of the declared constant, and require the boundary to fall exactly where the constant says. A done-when sharing only a file path, a symbol name and a numeric threshold with its plan produces NO report, asserted with all three present together so a lenient threshold cannot pass; that is the legitimate-pointer case and it is the one that decides whether the check survives contact. A copied paragraph whose whitespace and line breaks have been reflowed is still reported, asserted against a fixture that differs from the plan only in whitespace. A done-when sharing no long span produces no report. A plan section that cannot be resolved or read produces no report and does not raise, and the dispatch proceeds unchanged, because a check that can break a dispatch is worse than the defect it looks for. The dispatch's own behaviour is otherwise identical with and without a report, asserted by comparing a dry-run result that reports against one that does not on every other field. Report base and head over the new file and the tests importing reckon.crew.dispatch, with failure ids either side and none added. Bound the run per file and never run the full suite.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_a_met_wait_is_ready_not_abandoned.py -q passes, and a run whose declared wait has already reached one of its terminal states classifies as ready to resume and stays in the collection the resume sweep walks, rather than classifying as a dead worker. THE GAP, measured by another fleet against the code this repository landed an hour ago. That change made a declared wait outrank worker liveness, and it holds for a wait whose external condition is still PENDING: one run with a waiting manifest, a dead process and a running job classifies as waiting and the sweep counts it. It fails for a wait whose condition is already MET: a sibling run with a waiting manifest, all five wait fields well-formed, a dead process and a job that COMPLETED in two minutes classifies as abandoned with the detail that the process is gone without a complete manifest, and the sweep does not count it at all. So the discriminator has moved one step rather than disappearing, and it now falls exactly on the case the sweep exists for — the job finished, so the run should resume, and instead it leaves the set that would have woken it. A coordinator recovered it by hand. WHY THE EXISTING FALSIFIER DID NOT CATCH IT, which is the lesson to encode rather than just the bug to fix. The landed test asserts one manifest fixture twice, differing only in process liveness, and requires the same classification both ways. That ranges over liveness and NOT over the wait's own condition state, so every fixture it uses has a pending condition and the met case cannot appear. The property under test is two-dimensional and the test covered one dimension. This project has now shipped this same shape three times: a guard whose falsifier ranged over the population where the failure could not occur. WHAT TO CHANGE. When a manifest declares a wait, read the declared condition's state before concluding anything from process liveness, and classify on the pair. A pending condition with a dead process stays waiting, which is today's behaviour and must not regress. A MET condition — the probe reporting one of the states the manifest's terminal list names — is a run whose wait is over and whose recovery is to resume; give it the classification whose recovery verb is resume, and make sure it is in whatever collection the resume sweep consumes. Do not invent a new classification if an existing one already carries the resume verb and the right meaning; the vocabulary landed with several, and adding a fourth word for a state one of them already names is noise. Keep the overdue-wait handling and the declared-horizon judgement exactly as they are. THE PROBE IS THE INPUT AND IT MUST NOT BE TRUSTED BLINDLY. The manifest carries the probe as an argv array and the terminal states as a list, so the condition's state is obtainable, but a probe can fail, time out, print nothing, or print something matching no terminal state. Each of those is UNKNOWN, not met and not unmet: a run whose probe cannot answer must stay waiting rather than become abandoned, because a probe failure says nothing about the worker and abandoned is the state this project reserves for proof of death. Say that in a comment. Do not let a probe failure block or slow the classifier: it must remain a cheap read that cannot fail, so bound the probe and degrade to waiting on any fault. WHAT NOT TO TOUCH. Do not edit reckon/mcp_views.py, reckon/_backends.py or reckon/crew/promotion.py; peers hold all three. Do not change the wait field contract, the manifest schema, or the composed prompt. FALSIFIERS, in tests/test_a_met_wait_is_ready_not_abandoned.py, every probe stubbed, no test launching a real command or reading the real configuration home or live-pointer directory. RANGE OVER BOTH DIMENSIONS AS A GRID, which is the whole point: for each combination of process alive and process dead, against each of condition pending, condition met, and condition unknown, assert the classification, and assert it from one manifest fixture varying only those two inputs. Six cells, stated explicitly. A dead process with a met condition classifies to the type whose recovery verb is resume, and NOT to abandoned, asserted against abandoned's own value directly. A dead process with a pending condition still classifies waiting, pinning today's behaviour against regression. A dead process whose probe cannot answer classifies waiting and NOT abandoned. A met condition appears in the collection the resume sweep consumes, asserted by calling that path rather than by inspecting the classification, because the classification being right while the sweep set is wrong is the exact shape that lost two runs today. A probe that raises and a probe that times out both yield the unknown cell and do not raise. The classifier's probe invocation is bounded, asserted by a stub that would hang without a bound. Every existing recovery and state-typing test passes with its assertions unchanged. Report base and head over the new file, tests/test_recovery_state_typing.py, and the recovery and wait and resumption test files, with failure ids either side and none added. Bound the run per file and never run the full suite.

node_definition.done_when: pytest tests/test_a_resume_does_not_inherit_its_baseline.py -q passes, and a resumed run's manifest is read rather than discarded, so a manifest a previous attempt wrote is no longer treated as absent by the attempt that inherited it. THE DEFECT, measured on a live peer fleet's runs at the current head with two adjacent fixes already merged. The classifier gates a manifest on freshness: the manifest must be newer than a baseline mtime recorded on the run. On a resumed run that baseline is captured from the manifest the PREVIOUS attempt wrote, so the inherited manifest's mtime equals the baseline exactly, is not newer, is judged stale, and is treated as absent. Measured on one run at attempt six: baseline 1788874593998173197 and manifest mtime 1788874593998173197, identical, and the tool reported no manifest status while the file plainly read status waiting with five well-formed wait fields. WHY IT IS WORSE THAN ONE MISREAD RUN. Across five live runs in that fleet, FOUR had their manifests discarded this way. One was a parked run whose file said waiting and which classified abandoned, left the collection the resume sweep walks, and sat wakeable and unwoken while its external job had already completed; a coordinator recovered it by hand. The other three had files saying failed or blocked and classified running, which is the same discard with an outcome that looks harmless and therefore went unnoticed in that coordinator's own table. So the defect is not that a parked run is misread. It is that A RESUMED RUN'S MANIFEST IS DISCARDED WHATEVER IT SAYS, and the parked case is merely where the fallback to process liveness is dangerous. Two earlier fixes for the parked symptom are already merged and neither can fire, because both require the classifier to see a declared wait and the manifest is discarded before the wait is read. WHAT TO CHANGE, AND WHAT NOT TO. Fix the baseline, not the gate. A resume must not adopt its predecessor's manifest as its own baseline: the baseline exists to answer whether THIS attempt has written anything, and an inherited manifest answers whether ANY attempt ever wrote anything, which is a different question and the wrong one. Exempting a waiting status from the freshness gate would leave that wrong answer in place everywhere else the baseline is consulted, and the three misclassified terminal rows above are that everywhere-else already visible. So do not special-case any status. THE BASELINE A RESUME MUST USE, stated rather than left to you: every attempt in one run's chain shares the baseline recorded at that run's FIRST dispatch, and a resume inherits that baseline value rather than recomputing one from its predecessor's manifest. Carry the original value forward on each resume. That serves both purposes at once and the comment must say so: a manifest written by ANY attempt of this run is newer than the first dispatch, so it is read whatever its status, which is the behaviour being restored; and a manifest predating the run entirely is still older than that baseline, so the gate keeps doing the one job it was built for. The distinction the gate was reaching for is not attempt-versus-attempt, it is this-run-versus-before-this-run, and a resume genuinely inherits its predecessor's manifest as a handover rather than meeting it as a stale artefact. Do not use the resume's own start time as the baseline: a parked run's manifest is written by the attempt that parked and therefore predates every later resume, so a start-time baseline discards exactly the case this node exists to fix. WHAT NOT TO TOUCH. Do not change the waiting classification, the met-wait condition handling, the recovery vocabulary or the resume sweep's membership: all three landed today and their tests must keep passing unchanged. Do not edit reckon/crew/promotion.py, reckon/mcp_views.py or reckon/crew/dispatch.py. Do not change what a worker writes or the manifest schema. FALSIFIERS, in tests/test_a_resume_does_not_inherit_its_baseline.py, every fixture synthesised, no test reading the real configuration home or live-pointer directory. RANGE OVER ATTEMPT NUMBER AND OVER MANIFEST STATUS AS A GRID, because the defect was found through one status and affects all of them: for a first attempt and for a resumed attempt, against manifest statuses of complete, blocked, failed and waiting, assert the manifest is READ in every cell, from one fixture varying only those two inputs. Eight cells, stated explicitly. A resumed run whose inherited manifest has an mtime exactly equal to the recorded baseline is read rather than discarded, asserted with the two values set equal, since equality rather than staleness is the measured trigger. The gate still does its original job: a manifest written BEFORE the current attempt began and carrying a terminal status from an earlier attempt is not credited to the current attempt as its outcome, asserted by a fixture where that distinction is the only difference, so the fix cannot be a blanket removal of the gate. A parked resumed run classifies into the waiting family and appears in the collection the resume sweep consumes, asserted by calling that path, which is the end-to-end statement of the recovered behaviour. The three terminal-status cases classify from their manifests rather than from process liveness. Every existing recovery, state-typing and met-wait test passes with its assertions unchanged. Report base and head over the new file, tests/test_recovery_state_typing.py, tests/test_a_met_wait_is_ready_not_abandoned.py and the recovery and resumption test files, with failure ids either side and none added. Bound the run per file and never run the full suite.

REPAIR THE FUNCTION, NOT A CALLER. dispatch.py:3840 _backend_settings returns {launch, command} from argv[0] the moment a recorded argv is present, BEFORE it consults config, discarding the window, the model and the effort. Make that branch merge: argv supplies the command, config supplies the rest, neither discards the other.

ONE CANDIDATE IS ALREADY DEAD - do not spend a measurement rediscovering it. Passing a config to _backend_settings from promotion.py:1483 changes nothing, because the argv branch returns first. Measured with a positive control: live pointers 37 of 37 carry top-level argv, ledger rows 0 of 977 do (977 cli rows). promotion.py:1483 reads the live pointer, so the short-circuit fires every time. The same short-circuit silently defeats the three dispatch.py callers at 3559, 3908 and 4194 that ALREADY pass a real config - repairing the function fixes those too, which is the larger half and is invisible from 1483. It also carries the fifth caller resumption.py:407 without editing it, which is why resumption.py is not in your write scope.

DONE WHEN, and every clause emits evidence:

(1) A backend rebuilt from a recorded argv resolves utilisation against the configured window. Assert through the dispatch path AND through promotion.py:1483, which feeds StreamMeasures and writes the promoted row's input_utilisation_pct. Both sites are in this one write scope and are asserted at the combined state; a worker asserting only its own half cannot see what the pair does. Report the test node ids and their pass count.

(2) An unresolvable window yields unknown utilisation, never an announced or constant fallback. Demonstrate this as a refusal - a test that fails if the code substitutes any figure - and report its node id.

(3) A resumed run carries its recorded model and effort: assert the mapping resume_plan hands launch_plan contains both, taken from the recorded argv rather than a provider default. Report the assertion and its result.

(4) A resumed run is context-checked or says so explicitly. _context_fit_verdict has exactly one call site, routing.py:1601, inside dispatch resolution; the resume path never reaches it. Prefer an explicit unchecked state reported from resume_plan. routing.py is NOT in your write scope - if you find routing genuinely required, block and say so rather than reaching outside the fence. Silence does not satisfy this clause: silence is indistinguishable from a check that passed.

(5) State as digits how many of the five _backend_settings callers lose a setting before the change and how many after. The second figure is zero.

A RECORDED ROW'S WINDOW IS NEVER RESOLVED BY LOOKUP. If you touch historical rows, take the window from that row's own agent.usable_input_window. Resolving an alias against current config is correct ONLY for a run being dispatched now. Measured: alias dsv4-flash carries true windows 1016576 AND 492288; dsv4.1-flash carries 172800 AND 1016576, because a row holds what was configured when it ran and the configuration has moved twice. An alias lookup gets exactly the nine understating rows wrong again, for a new reason. These are two different requirements and conflating them reintroduces the defect.

THE FALSIFIER RANGES OVER WINDOW SIZES, NOT JUST DIRECTIONS, AND NEVER OVER THE LIVE LANE INVENTORY. Census of 983 ledger rows: 125 divide by something other than the window recorded beside them - 111 at window 1016576 over divisor 200000 (overstates about fivefold), 5 more the same, 6 at window 172800 over divisor 200000 (UNDERSTATES), 3 at window 492288 over divisor 1016576 (UNDERSTATES about twofold). The worst understatement reports 81.9 percent where the true figure is 94.8. Understatement is the direction that admits a node which should be held, and it lands on the SMALLEST window in the fleet - unsafe exactly where headroom is scarcest and safe where it is plentiful. So carry at least one fixture window BELOW the divisor and one ABOVE, and report both results as numbers. A test asserting only that the overstatement collapses passes while leaving the understating path untouched.

THE SINGLE-MODEL FIXTURE TRAP. The local lane serves exactly one model, so a fixture built from configured lanes cannot express the model defect at all. The model survives today only because the lane's --settings payload carries a modelPicker with replaceBuiltInOptions true offering one option; nothing in the code preserves it. Build a synthetic config carrying at least two models. Use effort as the positive control: --effort is dropped on EVERY lane, so an effort assertion fails against the unrepaired function even with a single-model fixture. Prove the test is aimed with effort before trusting the model assertion. Say this in the test docstring so narrowing it back is a visible edit.

Evidence you may assert against rather than reconstruct: a row promoted 13:10:37Z reads input_budget_tokens 200000 and input_utilisation_pct 64.9 against peak_input_tokens 129784, while agent.usable_input_window reads 1016576 in the same record. A live resumed worker's /proc argv carried --resume with --model and --effort both absent, where its dispatch argv had --model deepseek-v4-flash --effort high.

OUT OF SCOPE, do not repair here: 46 of 983 ledger rows are retried and carry no exclusion reason, so they reach effort calibration with an effort the attempt may not have used. That fix is a clause in ledger.measurement_exclusion_reason and belongs to another session. The trap if you touch it: capabilities._redispatched() returns True for resume (38), redispatch (6) and lane-change (2) alike via an attempt>1 fallback, and a redispatch re-runs with fresh argv so its recorded effort IS accurate.

Judge by delta against a stated base: record the base revision and its failure ids, and report added failures as a digit. Zero added against a red base is a pass. Gate the focused set covering dispatch.py and promotion.py plus your new test file, and capture it to one log; no full suite. Author your own landing record - a comment on the plan section and an anchor in the cumulative evidence record - and commit both in your worktree. Conventional commit subject AND a body.

node_definition.done_when: Confirm the defect first and quote both the source line and your own population figure in the manifest. reckon/crew/dispatch.py writes 'session_reuse': bool(backend.get('session_reuse')) at lines 3175 and 4351, copying the BACKEND CONFIG FLAG onto the run record. RE-MEASURE IT YOURSELF rather than trusting those numbers, because the population moves and a figure quoted from a document is exactly the fuse this repository warns about. WHY IT MATTERS, and state this back in your own words: a coordinator diagnosing a dead worker reads session_reuse as evidence that a long-lived session was re-admitted, and it answers true whether or not anything was resumed. That happened here today and produced a confident wrong root cause which a peer fleet had to refute with three facts. A field that is always true is worse than an absent one, because a reader reaches for it and it answers. Repair so the record distinguishes what the backend PERMITS from what this run DID. A run resumed when its own launch carried a prior session into argv; it did not when it minted a fresh one, which its first system init line shows. Keep the capability visible if it is useful, but not under a name a reader will take for an observation. Falsifier, which must fail at base: a run launched without a prior session reports that it did not resume, while a run launched with one reports that it did, asserted on the record rather than on the config. Range over the domain rather than one backend: a backend permitting reuse with no prior session, the same backend with one, and a backend not permitting it. Positive controls: the dispatch path is otherwise unchanged, a member's captured session is still recorded where it already is, and no existing reader of the run record breaks. node_definition.done_when: A peer project lost its entire roster to a silent write: 87 members to 0 at commit 490b5cc5, in a promote commit, exit 0, nothing reported. It surfaced six hours later as a dispatch refused for a member the coordinator had registered and used earlier the same session, and member add then rebuilt from zero, so the repair mechanism became a second writer of the corrupted state. Runs and holds in the same document survived. THE MECHANISM IS NOT KNOWN and you are not being asked to find it. Four candidates were ruled out here already, and record in your manifest that you did not re-derive them: the envelope loader raises on a corrupt file rather than defaulting, all four ledger.write callers pass a dict that preserves members, write refuses a stale expected_version, and no module outside ledger.py writes that document. Build the guard instead, because it is correct whether or not the cause is ever found. Refuse a write whose member count is lower than the member count of the version it is replacing, unless the caller states an intent to remove. Add that intent as an explicit parameter so a genuine removal stays possible and is visible at the call site. Falsifier, which must fail at base: a write carrying fewer members than the stored state raises rather than succeeding, and the stored roster is unchanged afterwards. Range over the domain rather than the 87-to-0 case: a drop to zero, a drop of one, a drop combined with an addition so the net is negative, and a same-count write that replaces one member with another, which must be REFUSED too if your rule is count-only, so decide whether identity or count is the thing guarded and say which you chose and why. Positive controls, all required: an ordinary registration that adds a member still succeeds, a re-registration of an existing member still succeeds, an explicit removal with the new intent parameter succeeds, and a write to a project with no ledger yet still creates one from empty without tripping the guard, since an absent ledger legitimately has zero members. Build every fixture in a temp directory and assert the real crew config home and the real docs directories are untouched. Gate: PYTHONPATH=$PWD /home/ITER/mcintos/Code/reckon/.venv/bin/python -m pytest -p no:cacheprovider -q your new file plus tests/test_ledger.py tests/test_roster_write_commits.py tests/test_crew_members.py tests/test_crew.py, captured to one log and reported as added failures against your base sha rather than as an absolute green; that cohort carries pre-existing failures.

It synthesises a temporary repository and pointer under tmp_path and never reads or writes the real crew home, asserting afterwards that the real pointer directory is untouched. Four cases, all holding at the repaired head. (a) A run whose manifest is status complete, commits empty, and whose changed_paths name only absolute paths outside the repository root promotes through the same entry point 'reckon crew complete' reaches, instead of raising the missing-commit refusal. (b) A manifest naming one path under the repository root with no commits is STILL refused with that message. (c) A mixed manifest naming one in-repository path beside out-of-repository paths is still refused, because the in-repository path still needs its commit. node_definition.done_when: the review for r-20260917T145144464105-a-run-record-says-whether-it-resumed parses all five score dimensions. That run split one field into two: the backend's capability, renamed to session_reuse_capable, and a new session_resumed recording what the run actually did. The defect it closes is that the old field read true on every live pointer on this workstation while most carried no session at all, and a coordinator read it as evidence and published a wrong root cause a peer fleet had to refute. Judge three things. Whether session_resumed is derived from the run's own launch rather than from config, since deriving it from the same source would reproduce the defect under a new name. Whether any existing reader of the old field name was left pointing at a key that no longer exists, which would be a silent break rather than a rename. And whether the rename is complete across the record's writers, since the run touched two call sites and a partial rename leaves two fields disagreeing. The node reports its falsifier failing 5 at base and passing 5 at head, which is the right shape; confirm it rather than assume it.

node_definition.done_when: the review for r-20260917T145149093479-a-refused-promotion-writes-nothing parses all five score dimensions. That run hoisted validation ahead of the plan write in promotion, where the landing comment was written fifty lines before the gate-evidence guard that rejects the call, so one malformed promotion left the plan dirty, a second guard then fired on that dirt, and a third refused because the comment already on disk carried different narrative text. Judge whether a refusal now leaves the plan byte-identical INCLUDING plan-version, since a version bump with no content change is the silent half of the original defect. Judge whether the immediately following retry succeeds with no intervening commit or cleanup, which is the property the cascade actually cost. And check the outcome coupling the worker reports preserving: it assigns the run's outcome after the comment reports recording the narrative, so confirm a published ledger row is unchanged rather than taking that on trust. Note on reading its manifest: the commits field is a YAML list of mappings and the reader currently flattens each item to a string carrying its own key, so use the sha from the mapping rather than the parsed value.

That run repaired a block-continuation test which treated any indented line as continuing an open block, so in a wholly indented manifest every field after a block scalar was folded into its value and commits came back empty. Commits is the field a promotion verifies a run by. Judge whether the new rule ends a block at the column where the surrounding fields sit rather than at column zero, and whether it was ranged over indent widths and tabs rather than the single two-space specimen in the brief. Two siblings landed in the same reader today, one keeping nested keys inside their parent and one still running on lists of mappings; check that this repair does not fight either, in particular that a block scalar nested under a parent still terminates correctly.

node_definition.done_when: Three fleets wrote three different filters over the same watch logs this week and got different answers, which is the defect. Establish the two failure modes yourself from the data before building: read the event files under ~/.config/reckon/crew/watch/ and confirm both halves. Filtering on event equal to transition DROPS genuine arrivals, because a dispatch a follower first sees is recorded as baseline with a null from_state, having no prior state to transition from; a peer fleet measured three real dispatches lost this way and came close to telling another fleet its own self-report was wrong. Accepting every baseline row INVENTS arrivals, because a follower re-attaching re-inventories the whole fleet and emits one row per live run within the same second. The correct discriminator is FIRST APPEARANCE PER NODE, not event class: the earliest row for a node is its arrival whatever its class, later baseline rows for that node are re-inventory, and transitions after the first row are real state changes. Build that as a reusable extraction in reckon/crew/query.py returning arrivals and state changes with their stamps. DO NOT wire a command into reckon/cli.py: that file is outside your scope, and state in the manifest what the entry point should look like so the caller can add it. STAMPS ARE THE OTHER HALF OF THIS and are not optional: the event files are mixed-format, carrying rendered ticker rows in LOCAL time alongside JSON rows, and a coordinator merging the two naively today manufactured a descending limb out of a concurrent ascent. Every stamp your extraction returns is UTC, explicitly, and a row whose zone cannot be established is reported as unknown rather than assumed. Falsifier, which must fail at base: over a fixture carrying a follower restart, the extraction returns each node exactly once as an arrival and no re-inventory row is counted, while a genuine dispatch recorded as baseline IS counted. Range over the domain rather than one file: a node appearing first as baseline, first as transition, appearing in two separate follower sessions, and a node whose only row is a re-inventory. Positive controls: real state changes after the first row are preserved in order, and a file with no baseline rows at all yields the same arrivals it does today. Gate: PYTHONPATH=$PWD /home/ITER/mcintos/Code/reckon/.venv/bin/python -m pytest -p no:cacheprovider -q your new file plus tests/test_crew_watch_stream.py tests/test_follow_observes_other_sessions.py tests/test_crew_monitor_output.py, captured to one log and reported as added failures against your base sha rather than as an absolute green.

node_definition.done_when: tests/test_review_call_sites.py passes and asserts five things. The review prompt at reckon/crew/prompts/review.md names a sixth required emission, CALL_SITES, whose line lists the production call sites the reviewer reached the change through, or the literal none when it found none, and states that production excludes the change's own test files; the prompt states the requirement is not optional, in the same terms the checklist already uses for an omitted item reading exactly like a checked one. parse_review records call_sites as a list and call_site_count as an integer, with an emission of none recording an empty list and a count of zero, and an omitted CALL_SITES line recording the item as absent rather than as zero, because absent and zero are different claims and only one of them is a measurement. A stored record carrying call_site_count 0 is machine-filterable without reading its prose, asserted by filtering a set of synthesised records rather than by string matching. reckon.crew.recovery._review_is_complete still returns True for every one of the 151 stored reviews that predate this field, asserted by calling it on a record with no call-sites key at all, because other sessions' live scoring runs depend on that predicate not moving. node_definition.done_when: Two changes in reckon/crew/promotion.py, and the first test must FAIL against today's code. First, _restore_landing_writes at line 1626 treats a non-zero return from git restore --source=HEAD --staged --worktree as proof that the path was created by this promotion and may be unlinked. Replace that inference with a direct query: ask git whether HEAD carries the path, using git cat-file -e with the path prefixed by HEAD and a colon, and unlink only when that query says HEAD does not carry it. A path HEAD carries stays on disk whatever the restore returned. THE TEST THAT MATTERS asserts a path PRESENT in HEAD survives a restore that failed for an unrelated reason: drive the git runner so the restore invocation returns non-zero for a reason unrelated to the path's presence, over a tracked file HEAD carries, and assert the file is still on disk. Written the obvious way round, that a path absent from HEAD is dropped, the test passes while preserving the defect, so keep that as a SECOND case covering the behaviour the fallback legitimately exists for, and state in the manifest which of the two fails at base. Second, any failure raised after the ledger append has succeeded must name it, in this shape: the ledger row for the run is already written, do not re-promote. The append happens before the pointer delete, so a message reading could not stage the landing writes with exit status 0 invites exactly the retry that produced a duplicate row today. Reproduce both at base and paste the figures into the manifest: with index.lock held, git restore exits 128, which is the measured shared cause between the failure that triggers the rollback and the failure of the rollback. Ruff check and format over exactly the staged paths add no findings beyond the same paths at the base revision, with both counts pasted as digits. DO NOT PROMOTE THIS NODE and do not run crew complete on it: the defect being fixed lives on the promote path, so promoting the repair runs it on the way in. Land by ordinary git commit of the named paths only.
